speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the recommendation of the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements against any reduction in general federal support for post-secondary education, and in view of the concern expressed by many students in Ottawa today that post-secondary education not be relegated to a purely economic concern, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong):
That this House instructs the government to forget whatever notions of cutbacks in this sector it may have, and that this House affirms its appreciation of the value of a liberal arts education and critical thinking in general as the best guarantee of sound and democratic social and economic policy.

Moshe Dayan, a military man who spent many years fighting for a cause, and who, in the last few years of his life worked so tirelessly to establish peace in the Middle East, will be greatly missed by all of us who wish to see an end to hostilities in that region of the world. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the minister allegedly responsible for housing. Another report did emerge on the weekend from CMHC, this one contending that 135 families a day between now and the fall of 1983 will lose their homes. The Toronto Star has a copy of the report, and I have a copy of the report. I find it astounding that the minister should get to his feet today and say, as he did just a minute ago, that he has not even looked at it or has not seen it. I would like to send him over a copy. He can have a look at it, and I hope, prepare himself for tomorrow's question period.
Since this has been an issue of profound concern in every community across Canada for the past few months, and since it has been raised in this House ever since it opened last week, why has the minister not taken the trouble to read the report, and why does he not report back to the House of Commons on its accuracy?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition, I already indicated that this morning in Metropolitan Toronto I met with a group of representatives of Canadian home owners affected by high interest rates, who asked to make submissions to me; this was not a report from staff but actually people who are impacted by high interest rates. They asked to make a submission to me. I met with them. I then got on an airplane and came directly to this building.
I have not read this report, but I have indicated that, from the newspaper reports which say that by 1983 100,000 people will lose their homes, the report is wildly out of date. It is erroneous. It talks about starts in the first quarter as being
135.000	when we all know they are at 180,000, so it is over
30.000	out to begin with. If the hon. member, through his research staff, cannot do any better than that and cannot come up with something better than that, I think he should dig in a bit deeper.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the report was done it was done on the assumption that mortgage rates would be at 21 per cent. They have only dropped to 19.75 per cent. I say that even the minister should be able to calculate that if the data that went into his report was accurate-he has not yet taken the trouble to read this report prepared by his staff and he should have read it weeks ago and not have to wait until it is raised in the House-this slight drop in the level of mortgage rates will not mean "boo" all in terms of the number of families who will lose their homes by next fall.
Since the report indicates that rent levels are going to climb astronomically next year as well, and since the minister in a CTV interview last April said he was opposed to the continuation of rent controls, and made the same point in a speech somewhere else last year, I would like him to take the opportunity to clarify the government's position. Is the minister now in favour of his old position, which is to abolish rent controls, which will be disastrous, or will he admit he was mistaken?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Two weeks ago Manitobans were heartened when the American Ambassador to Canada told us that the Garrison Diversion Unit, as it is now planned, would be scrapped. He promised documentation from President Reagan confirming his statement. However, last Thursday in Fargo, North Dakota, Interior Secretary James Watt told North Dakota farmers that he and the President supported Garrison. speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

subsubtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY UNITED STATES ADMINISTRATION

speechtext:

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Mines responsible for the Status of Women in Canada, whom I also wish to congratulate at this time. I wish to ask her what the government intends to do about restoring the rights of Mrs. Sandra Lovelace of the Tobique Indian Reserve and those of thousands of Indian women like her in Canada, following the decision made this summer by the United Nations Human Rights Commission. Does the government intend to ratify the appropriate instrument at the United Nations and change the Indian Act?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. Yes, indeed, Canada is in contravention of an existing convention because of the Indian Act, and it is an embarrassment to me and to every woman of this country. Just recently the cabinet ratified a decision to sign the United Nations convention which will effectively eliminate all forms of discrimination against women as soon as possible. We did so on the basis of the charter of rights. The cabinet has instructed the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to consult with the Indian people of this country in order to develop a mechanism by which amendments can be made as quickly as possible.
I might add that the support of the members of this House, and the support of the women of Canada, will be with us in the swift passage of the charter of rights and the constitutional package.

Hear, hear!

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. subsubtopic: RESPONSIBILITY OF FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS TO FARMERS
speechtext: My question is for the Minister of Agriculture and is with regard to enormous pressures on Canadian farmers caused, on one hand, by high interest rates and high input costs, and on the other by the lack of compensating higher incomes. The minister has been saying for months that Canadian lending institutions, specifically banks, have a responsibility to their farm customers. First, I should like to ask the minister what he regards this responsibility to be; second, how may we be assured this alleged responsibility by Canadian banks is being or will be discharged properly?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: RESPONSIBILITY OF FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
In this country the responsibility with lending institutions is very great. When we investigated, we found that of the people who made representations to my ministry, 90 percent had been improperly lent money by the banks for term capital investment. The banks lent them huge amounts of money on demand notes and floating loans that should have been on 10 or 20-year mortgages. When interest rates increased they could not meet the payments. It is mostly in one sector of agriculture, and that is the red meat industry. The beef and pork production entities are in great difficulty. The horrible lending policies of most lending institutions is the problem. Under the present Bank Act we say there is room to lend the farmers the money on long-term financing and at reasonable rates of interest, giving them a moratorium on a 20-year mortgage of three years, and amortizing the first three years without capital or interest,
Oral Questions
until they organize themselves into a better marketing system. It is those farmers outside of a proper marketing system who are in financial difficulty today.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: If the lending institutions, as the minister alleges, are at the worst ripping off their farm customers, or at the least not discharging their proper responsibility to those farm customers, can the minister tell us exactly what he wants the banks to do? Has that been communicated in exact terms to the banks? If not, when will it be, either by the minister directly or through his colleague, the Minister of Finance? What mechanism does the Minister of Agriculture propose to make sure that that, in fact, is what happens vis-a-vis the relationship between the banks and their farm customers?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Under the present Bank Act, Madam Speaker, there is room for them to move. I have had meetings with the heads of the Canadian banking institutions as far back as May, when we became concerned with representations that farm organizations and farmers made to us about some of the things they foresaw happening. I have hundreds of letters where they made appeals to me about their financial situation. We have gone over this with the Canadian Bankers' Association. We met the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association less than two weeks ago. We discussed the very things I have mentioned to the hon. member. I also had the same kind of discussions with my colleagues, especially the Minister of Finance. We will have to be patient and wait until November 3.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, certain amendments to Bill C-48 have been proposed and presented to the House for determination. These amendments include a definition of a "spill"; the inclusion of an "authorized spill" in the provisions of the bill as equal in implication to that of "accidental spill"; the requirement of reporting a spill and informing those people likely to be affected; the liability for economic loss or damage resulting from a spill; the composition and use of a compensation fund; and the reduction in the absolute discretionary powers of the minister to make determinations affecting environmental considerations and the people who populate Canada lands.
In advancing and discussing these amendments and their ramifications, the intent is to strengthen and enhance this part of the bill which reflects acknowledgement of the larger and larger proportion that environmental protection assumes in the responsibilities of governments, industry and individuals.
Last week's distribution of the report of the subcommittee on acid rain gives emphasis and impetus to the environmental character of everything we undertake. It is entitled "Still Waters-The Chilling Reality of Acid Rain". It is a demand for more than lip service notation of this specific environmental disaster. The intent of the debate today and last week is that the same demand for adequate attention be put to the government.
In the report "Still Waters", the subcommittee recommends that the following elements be included in environmental protection legislation to effectively reduce pollution in general and particularly acid rain air pollution. First, the imposition of penalties high enough to ensure that there is no benefit from saved cost of compliance in case of non-compliance; second, the creation of a tribunal which would have exclusive jurisdiction over environmental law prosecution; and, further, the provision of a funding mechanism for class actions which would otherwise not be instituted due to inadequate financial resources on the part of the initiators.
Pending consideration and implementation of the reforms advocated in the previous recommendations, the subcommittee recommended that effective steps be taken to apply existing environmental protection legislation.
Last spring the Special Committee on Alternative Energy and Oil Substitution released a report entitled "Energy Alternatives". There, too, environmental anxieties were expressed in the section entitled "Environmental Concerns" on page 59, as follows:
The exploitation of energy cannot be accomplished without having some effect upon the environment, but different energy options affect the environment in differing ways and degrees ... It would not make sense to formulate an energy policy which would solve energy problems but create serious environmental ones.
That refers to energy alternatives.
In light of some of the provisions of Bill C-48 we must ask how the concerns of these special committees will be serviced with any degree of confidence and certainty. How will the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) possibly fulfil these recommendations which are within his mandate when, in fact, he can only act and react with the sanction of his superior minister? Where does this bill demand that environmental impact studies be a mandatory part of exploration and development? It does not, Mr. Speaker. It allows that the minister-not the minister responsible for environmental matters but the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-may require certain things. This, of course, will only be after considering his primary function and his ministerial responsibilities.
How is this discretionary power implanted in one person, one office-I think I should say two, in deference to the other minister who is present-translated into positive action for protection of this narrow envelope which encircles the globe we live on? One man, and one man only, will decide.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to this important piece of legislation which bears such implications for the future of Canada. Our society, like every modern society, moves, manufactures, builds, farms, communicates, warms, cools, lives, on the basis of its energy supply and distribution. It may be trite to comment on the happy circumstance in which we Canadians find ourselves, with a variety and volume of energy sources unmatched in the world. It is also trite and increasingly unnecessary to remind ourselves and Canadians generally that the only impediment to a parallel, unmatched prosperity in Canada is that imposed by the policies of the government. It is a government which has had
October 19, 1981

nearly a quarter of a century of opportunity to enact its will upon the nation but there is unimpeachable evidence of a careless disregard for that trust. There is absolutely no valid excuse that can be advanced by hon. members opposite to explain and rationalize a situation in which Canadians sitting on absolute energy wealth are, nevertheless, petroleum supply dependent.
Just as it is Liberal government policy which has produced interest rates which are 4 per cent to 5 per cent higher than those in the United States, together with all the attendant social and economic woes which these irresponsibly invoked interest rates have imposed, so it is Liberal government "easy-way-out" energy policy and putting party interests before national interests that have produced the present unpleasant reality that Canada faces today regarding energy.
In this circumstance it ill-behooves the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) to frame her speech to this House last Wednesday with statements that contained, first and last, unworthy and uncouth criticism of members on this side of the House. No amount of such prima donna preening will lead Canadians to misinterpret the record of this government.
Before we discuss the proposed amendments to Bill C-48, Mr. Speaker, I think we should look at some of the remarks and accusations made by the Minister of State for Mines. Two questions were posed in the statement of that minister. The first was: How much has Conservative obstruction cost this country in terms of our stated goal of reaching energy self-sufficiency? The answer is not one day; not one dollar. The Canadian people know who has been the culprit in delay and in cost. The Canadian people understand the difference between the Conservative's 18 cents and the Liberal government's shameful betrayal in the form of 50-cent or 60-cent gasoline price increases.
The second question is: How many Canadian oil and gas companies have been denied an opportunity to participate in promising Canada lands exploration due to this opposition? Again, the answer to the minister's question is not one. The question should be turned around, rephrased and directed at the hon. minister and her government: How many dedicated, talented, hard-working Canadians, and how many drilling and servicing rigs have been forced out of Canada to the United States and to Australia by the policies of this administration? In the words of the minister, how much has this cost the country in terms of our stated goal of reaching energy self-sufficiency?
Perhaps forcing drilling and development activity out of Canada is this government's ultimate weapon in protecting the Canadian environment. Let me say that only when this government puts forward legislation which is above criticism and above improvement, and when the government starts listening to the people and allows elected members to participate meaningfully in the formulation and improvement of legislation, just that soon can it be expected that we will react in the manner that the hon. member for Nickel Belt seemed to
Canada Oil and Gas Act
suggest, namely, that this House should pass legislation quickly. Passage of bills will develop as we have confidence and as we can study and make suggestions. However, just so long as the attitude remains that the views of hon. members are a nuisance, relegated to the dark confines of committee from whence they can be ignored into oblivion, can it be expected that this House will be the forum for expression and opposition to imperial, impaired judgment.
The interpretation of "Trudeaumocracy" in this House does not impress us in the least, and it does not impress Canadians whose intelligence is continually misjudged and insulted. The constituents I am honoured to represent would most certainly support tough environmental conditions in this bill. They understand the pressures put upon an area's ecological balance by the influx of people and the influx of industrial and development activity. I believe that the people for whom I speak resent the degree of ministerial and bureaucratic judgment which can so often yield to an element of expediency, whether it be political or economic expediency.
The area which I represent has one of the most fragile ecological environments contained within our Canadian borders, with only 10 inches of annual precipitation, with a consequence that our lakes and our land receive little of the flushing, laving action which rains and snow provide. With the compaction of increasing numbers of citizens within its limited but favoured bounds, we can understand environmental concerns. We can understand and appreciate the necessity for those parts of this legislation concerned with protection of other environmentally vulnerable areas of Canada. I might say that we are impressed that recognition is given to the fact that adequate funding is one of the keys to protection of the environment. We will be making our case for similar financial recognition of the costs involved in protection of the Okanagan valley chain of lakes, affecting, as it does, the quality of lives for hundreds of thousands of citizens and tourists, and costs that exceed the resources which municipal and regional governments can muster.
Let me invite hon. members of this House to visit Okana-gan-Similkameen so they can develop an appreciation of why residents there are alert to protecting the ecology anywhere in Canada, including Canada lands. Come with me to view Vaseaux Lake, where more than 100 acres of lake surface is matted and destroyed for use by Eurasian milfoil. Come with me to Osoyoos; talk to Mayor Frost and his council, and talk to the chamber of commerce. Let them describe one community's uphill battle to preserve the integrity of their lake, with its attraction for tourists whose patronage is so essential to the economics of that area. Come with me to discuss environmental concerns with those who are alarmed by the possible uranium mining development.
Yes, the citizens of Okanagan-Similkameen are alert to the dangers which development brings to our area. We can understand and appreciate the reason for the environmental protection sections of this bill. We relate to the alarm stated by groups and individuals from lands covered by Bill C-48. That is why I must note that there are aspects of the environmental

provisions of this bill which require-I emphasize require- criticism and require change.
If the notation has been made by hon. members who have spoken previously, the implication must be that the error is so glaring and so gross, and the remedies are so apparent, the government is so obtuse, and the consequences are so grave, that the point must be made and made again. We challenge hon. members opposite to do something to remedy the flaws that provoke our attention. That is what we suggest.
, The guts of our complaint about the environmental inclusions in Bill C-48 is simply that there seems to be a determination to ensure that in the future environmental concerns will be addressed with the same effectiveness that the Liberal government's National Energy Program has addressed the whole area of energy self-sufficiency and pricing. Why else would Bill C-48 relegate the Minister of the Environment to such a subservient role in the only area of his competency and mandate, allowing him to act only upon the blessing of other ministers whose primary responsibilities deny a detached objectivity in this secondary role?
We have the emperor Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and now we will be provided with the czar of energy, spreading his jurisdiction into environmental areas of concern in which he will have a paramount vested interest. Surely such conflict simply ensures the mediocracy of environmental protection efforts. To this aspect we take umbrage. It was the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who, in presenting Bill C-48 to this House, acknowledged the importance of environmental protection in oil and gas exploration and said on December 11, in the first phase of this debate, that the bill contains:
-a whole series of provisions so that the government can be sure that exploration in the north and offshore is ecologically sound and that exploration work and the actual projects are respectful of the environment which, as everyone knows, is extremely fragile in these regions.
So said the minister-words, the intent of which is not totally borne out in the text of the bill.
On October 15, 1981, the same minister made this statement in the House:
-the minister will hold what 1 would call blank cheques from oil and gas operators which can be drawn to compensate claimants without proof of fault or negligence. This means that claimants will have two avenues open to them, one, the judicial process, the other a direct claim to the minister-
They will have the option of filing claims either before the courts or directly with the minister. That is wonderful, but it is noteworthy that the minister holds the power to respond. By his own admission he will merely allow the Minister of the Environment a corroborative role. That is the fallacy of the bill. The basic flaw is too much ministerial discretion. Where is the advocate for the environment? Where do the people who are most affected, the residents and the present occupiers of these Crown lands, have a voice and an effective instrument acting on their behalf? We now have a ministerial explanation of the purpose of the fund which is to be developed. Unfortunately, the bill does not explicitly state that purpose.
Canadians have learned only too well the degree to which they can rely on the word or the promise of this government and of those who speak on behalf of this government. As the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) noted on Friday, even if the present minister evoked great and general confidence, this act remains long after the present minister departs.
A recently leaked bulletin indicates the concern this government has regarding its loss of credibility with respect to energy pricing in light of its election promises to keep the price of gasoline low.

However, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, by the nature of his position, must weigh environmental protection against the need for development. EMR has an obvious first responsibility towards energy supply. That ambiguity can lead to conflict. Therefore, the Minister of the Environment should be the one in charge of the fund.
I must add that the possibility of this conflict occurring is intensified by the growing intimacy and relationship between the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and Petro-Canada, an intimacy evidenced by the appointment of Michael Phelps to the minister's staff while he benefits financially from a purported position within PetroCan. We ask specifically that the mandate of the Minister of the Environment be recognized, honoured and activated in fact and in act. speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak to the motions which have been grouped together for
October 19, 1981

this debate. Each of them deals with some aspect of oil and gas spills and the consequent threat of environmental damage.
Needless to say, the government is extremely sensitive to this danger and will continue to do everything within its power to prevent any such accidents. At the same time we are realists, and while we demand every care and caution, we must also be prepared for the worst should it ever happen. Appropriate measures have been designed to cope with any emergency that might arise.
As members are aware, the motions we are now debating are just eight of 57 on the Order Paper dealing with Bill C-48. That may sound like a lot, but I think it is a very healthy sign indeed. It reflects an awareness and real appreciation of the importance of legislation designed to bring long-term benefits to the country as a whole, and which has special significance for northern Canadians.
Each proposed amendment deserves our careful attention certainly. But in dealing with specific clauses and provisions we may run the risk of losing sight of the over-all thrust and objectives of the bill itself. For that reason, I would like to take this opportunity to give a somewhat broader focus to our deliberations and to correct certain persistent misconceptions.
As minister responsible for northern affairs, I am responsible for the political, economic and social development north of 60, for the over-all administration of northern resources and the co-ordination of federal activities in the two territories. Let me say categorically that nothing in Bill C-48 alters that responsibility in any way. It does, however, provide new opportunities for achieving northern objectives.
The bill will be administered jointly by my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and myself, but according to our respective jurisdictions. We have worked together closely in the preparation of this legislation; our two departments are pooling their talents and resources with the creation of the Canada oil and gas lands administration to achieve a shared national objective.
I think it would be worth while to expand on some of the provisions of Bill C-48 to ensure that there is no confusion in anyone's mind as to the responsibilities of my colleague the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and myself.
Because of the misconception that continues to be reiterated I will refer to the bill. The interpretation of "minister" under the two acts covered by Bill C-48 identifies the separate jurisdiction of the minister of northern development relevant to Canada lands in the territories and in the offshore of Canada's Arctic coast. Let us make no mistake that the ultimate political accountability in terms of Parliament for this bill for north of 60 falls on the shoulders of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

speechtext:
My colleague the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and I have agreed that the oil and gas management functions of our two departments will be pooled into the Canada oil and gas lands administration to be
Canada Oil and Gas Act
headed by an administrator who will be the designated official of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the minister of northern affairs, again relevant to each minister's respective jurisdiction as required by the bill.
The administrator will report to the deputy minister of energy, mines and resources and to the deputy minister of northern affairs, and at their direction will relate on policy matters to the assistant deputy minister of energy regarding energy policy and to the assistant deputy minister of northern affairs concerning northern policy. Northern policy includes energy policy north of 60.
A policy review committee including both assistant deputy ministers will provide policy guidelines and review all policy decisions of COGLA or the administrative body to ensure they are consistent with the requirements of energy policy and northern policy. The committee will be the instrument by which activities of the administrative body are integrated and harmonized with activities retained by both departments.
If I may reiterate, as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development I am directly accountable for the following: first, environmental management and protection including responsibility for the environmental studies fund north of the line of administrative convenience defined in Schedule VI of the Canada oil and gas regulations; second, socioeconomic benefits for the people resident in the territories; third, negotiating strategies and agreement with territorial governments; and fourth, co-ordination of policy and over-all planning in relation to major resource development north of 60.
The management, then, of oil and gas rights in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon and adjacent continental margins is but one element of my over-all responsibility in the north, and when I say "my" I am referring to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and any succeeding ministers.
I have also been assigned responsibility for safeguarding the northern environment, for social and constitutional development, and of course native land claims.
I do not know how political accountability to this Parliament for all those policies north of 60 could be more clear, as well as those of my colleague the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources south of 60, and the bill quite clearly states that.
In carrying out these responsibilities I want to emphasize that we must strive to achieve balance in development; balance between renewable and non-renewable resource development, balance between the conventional wage employment activities and those that support the traditional native economy, balance between externally generated development and that from within, balance between using the land and resources and conserving them, and, last, balance between protecting the environment and developing the natural resources available to us.

Canada Oil and Gas Act
Many members may be aware, particularly some members I see in this House-and perhaps they are very familiar with this-of a very recent and dramatic example of the kind of balance we have striven for and achieved as reflected in the government's decision respecting the Norman Wells oil field expansion and pipeline project this past summer. Of course, that was subject to a two-year delay in major construction. I say this decision is symbolic of the very thing I am talking about, the very mandate of this department as it was before C-48 and as it is to remain after C-48.
This decision was not arrived at lightly. In weighing the elements of the Norman Wells project the government asked the Federal Environmental Review Assessment Office, commonly referred to as FERAO, to consider not just the environmental factors but also the socioeconomic aspects of that project. The National Energy Board also studied the project, and both agencies held public hearings both north and south of 60 and reported positively, subject to specific terms and conditions.
I personally sought the views of northerners on this project through a series of public meetings held in Yellowknife and in the communities of the Mackenzie Valley last spring for this purpose, to achieve a governmental decision that could have balance between the local concerns and the industry's proposals, and reconciling those with the national interests. The decision on Norman Wells meets the criteria that I believe a northern resource project should meet.
Especially in view of the two-year delay, the pipeline project will be managed in a socially and environmentally acceptable manner, and at the same time it will provide enhanced job opportunities and economic benefits for northerners. I remind members as well that the decision to proceed with this project is subject to a delay in construction work toward meeting the concerns of the Dene and Metis regarding adequate time for negotiation of their land claim.
With respect to that project, by reconciling the interests of fulfilling that mandate the decision met with the approval, publicly declared at the time of the decision, of not only the territorial government and the Dene and Metis but, as to the resources, of the companies involved. This can be symbolic of what can be done to achieve a consensus on what on the surface would be conflicting interests, which have always been troublesome north of 60.
In this project and others, my department and I continue to meet our particular responsibilities to ensure that northerners benefit economically and socially from resource development in the north. With the co-operation of the territorial governments and the private sector, certain requirements have been laid down as a precondition for industry to undertake before commencing oil and gas activities. These conditions cover such areas as employment of northerners and protection of the environment.
To cite one notable example where this policy has produced very beneficial results indeed, I might refer to one development in the Beaufort Sea area. One company there has provided employment for 300 northerners and local economic benefits
in the order of $30 million. This has been accomplished by suasion and the co-operation of the industry; but also the enactment of this particular bill will enable a melding of resource management objectives with the other vital northern policy objectives such as employment and local business development.
Considerable progress has also been recorded through measures aimed at protecting the environment in areas of oil and gas operations. Exploratory drilling, whether on land or offshore, for instance, must conform with specific preconditions set by my department. Environmental impact studies have been required before many such activities have been approved.
Under legislation currently before the House, a revolving fund of $15 million will be set up by assessment on industry to cover the cost of such studies, to be conducted under the direction of my department. Complementary to the requirements of the Arctic Water Pollution Prevention Act, evidence of financial responsibility as well as the assumption of unlimited liability for damages will be required from industry for its offshore operations.
I cannot list here all the programs and initiatives related to oil and gas activities which have been undertaken in recent years. They deal with other considerations such as supplies to northerners of locally produced petroleum products, licensing policies, exploration agreements, technical developments and so on. But I think it should be clear to all members that even without Bill C-48 the government has had the interest and welfare of northerners clearly in mind in developing resource policies over the past two decades. That is a priority which will definitely, in my view, be strengthened by this proposed legislation.
In determining our strategies and directions we have counted heavily on the input of the northerners themselves. The extent of their participation is sometimes overlooked. It has ranged from frequent consultation on land use permits and socioeconomic plans to major discussions involved in the environmental impact assessment processes, and regional planning projects such as the Lancaster Sound study.
Nowhere is the contribution of northerners more evident nor, indeed, more appreciated than in the eight amendments to the bill accepted by the government in response to proposals introduced by the Inuit committee on national issues.
Briefly I should like to touch on at least some of these amendments which have so notably improved the bill itself. It was through the efforts of the Inuit committee that a key passage on aboriginal rights, Sections 5 to 7, was amended to read, and I quote:
Nothing in this act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this act.
This was the clause that satisfied so many of the Inuit who had previously expressed concern about the implications of the bill.
October 19, 1981

Another Inuit amendment provided that an exploration agreement "may require equity participation by government and Canadians," including any aboriginal peoples who may be affected. That also was a significant improvement in terms of opening up the potential for joint ventures in the resource field.
Again, the Inuit committee suggested that an exploration agreement "may require training and employment opportunities" for disadvantaged individuals or groups. I hardly think there would be any opposition to that particular amendment. I regard the development of the north as fundamental to the future of the north. I regard, then, the development of human resources in the north as fundamental to the future of the north.
A great many northerners have also voiced their concerns during meetings with me personally and in countless letters. I submit that the government has moved ahead with this legislation fully aware of northern rights. Personally, I would like to express my appreciation to the many people who have devoted so much time and effort in producing what 1 am convinced will be an effective piece of legislation.
For the skeptics who still see something sinister in this legislation, 1 would like to deal briefly with a few of the more persistent allegations. First, Bill C-48 does not prejudice decisions respecting native land claims. The notion that it seeks to remove oil and gas rights from the claim settlement process is simply incorrect. I reiterate, Section 5(7) affirms that nothing in this bill interferes with existing aboriginal rights. I stress that Clause 61, respecting the replacement of oil and gas licences and rights, refers only to mineral rights held under former legislation and will not prejudice native claims.
If there are those who still doubt the government's good faith with respect to land claim negotiations, let them cast an eye on the recent decisions not only on Norman Wells but the Petro-Canada exploration agreement. Construction of the pipeline extension and exploration activities were delayed for two years in those instances to allow for issues related to land claims to be resolved through negotiation.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in the House after a summer recess to address an environmental issue-I think that is the issue before us- not as an issue which represents the entirety of Bill C-48 but simply one subset in a set of six or seven amendments which have been proposed.
The environment is a topic about which I think it is generally quite difficult to get Canadians excited. Most Canadians in the present economic climate-and I think justifiably so- should be concerned about their capacity to hold on to their houses in the face of high interest rates or to their jobs in the face of increasing unemployment, which is a consequence of bad economic policies. Those issues are here and now issues because they represent our capacity to stay warm and cosy in the winter months and to have the sort of food which gives us and our families the kind of health we have come to expect in this country. However, environmental issues over the longer term are the sleeper issues. It is the destruction of the environment which will cause difficulty for all of us over the longer term.
As we approach something like Bill C-48 and the development of some of our energy resources in parts of Canada which are remote from our major cities, it behooves everyone in this chamber to do what he or she can to raise a degree of public consciousness about the importance for all of us of environmental issues over time. Perhaps in that context we should be a little more alert today than might be necessary in the future or might have been necessary in the past because it is my conviction that one of the tragedies of the present situation in Canada is that we have a government which has remained reasonably consistent since 1968, with one nine-
October 19, 1981

month exception. Therefore, we have a track record which we can look at, identify and project into the future.
There are many characteristics of the track record of the present government, but the one which I think must concern us in relation to environmental issues is this government's demonstrated record of caring not so much about what is good for Canadians but more about what is politically saleable at the moment, and the consequences for the future of this nation of that political saleability be darned.
If we look back to 1968 and track the decisions which have been made, we will find that characteristic. We find it as a consequence of some rather consistent attitudes. Whether we deal with social policy, in the way I have in the last 16 or 17 months as the employment critic for our party, or with other portfolios, such as the one I now hold respecting health and welfare, we find a rather consistent attitude on the part of the government in total, and some ministers more specifically than others, which ignores local advice.
If we look at this legislation and its clauses which deal with the environment, where do we find clauses which require a minister of the Crown, who resides a good part of each day and each week in the city of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, at least to be the recipient of local input? Where do we find in this proposed legislation any clause or phrase which provides for a substantial degree of local control? We are dealing with a piece of Canadian geography which is large, which is different from one part of it to another and which is not well understood by those of us born and raised in the southern part of this country, and I think that includes most of us.
During the brief exchange between the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), a member on our side of the House, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), I heard the words "clear water," and that reminded me of an experience I had 13 or 14 years ago when I drove from Window Rock, Arizona some considerable distance to a place called Toyee. I arrived on the scene at Toyee, Arizona to discover what looked like a small-sized town. This town contained a school which was a bureau of Indian affairs school. As I drove into the town I saw many houses, dormitory buildings and classrooms. The outstanding characteristic of Toyee which first occurred to me when I arrived was the fact that about two-thirds of the houses, dormitories and classrooms were boarded up.
You ask yourself why. They look relatively new. They are not old-fashioned buildings that have been around a long time and lost their usefulness. They looked recently constructed, yet they are boarded up. As you encounter the local people, the people who live in Toyee, and ask them why these buildings are boarded up, they tell you the English translation of the Navajo word "Toyee', is "place of no water". The local people understood their environment. They understood that fresh water in Toyee, Arizona, was in short supply.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
In Washington, D.C., in the United States of America, the bureaucrats, the minister responsible, in their wisdom built a community designed to handle about 1,500 people. The environment, the clean water, despite modern technology, could support but 500 people. Therefore, we have accommodation and classrooms for 1,000 people boarded up because the minister and the bureaucrats were not required and did not have the wisdom to consult with the local people before they built the school.
That is the aspect of Bill C-48 which clearly disturbs me as I attempt to read it and comprehend its implications. Before joining the House of Commons, I worked in a university. I have tremendous respect for the skills and knowledge of many of my colleagues in that setting. But regardless of their discipline, they too are captives of their background and experience. However broad and however deep those experiences are for us, they are always limited.
I suggest to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that he is the captive of his experiences. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is also the captive of his experiences. The issue of northern development will affect the lives of all Canadians and most clearly the lives of those who live in that region of our great country. In proposing legislation that governs that region of our country, or any region of our country, with respect to those clauses and phrases which concern a minister or those who follow him, one should always consult with the local people if dealing with a sparsely populated region of this country where few of us have any direct experience or any direct personal, long-term investment.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development stood in this House a few moments ago and said that the control of the environmental impact study responsibility and the funds allocated would reside in the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources south of 60 and in the Minister of Indian and Northern Development north of 60. There was a certain sense of pride as the minister implied he would take those responsibilities seriously.
I have a thought which comes out of my personal knowledge: fresh water flows back and forth across that parallel; air travels back and forth across that parallel. I have sat in the House long enough to know there are conflicts among ministers. All is not sweetness and light on every occasion. I wonder what there is about that region of our country as we approach the 60th parallel that leads us to believe, when it comes to an environmental issue, that it makes a modicum of sense to appoint one minister responsible for air and clean water north of 60 and a different minister responsible for air and clean water south of 60. Would any rational human being reach the conclusion that that kind of structure is the proper kind of structure? I hear my colleague say that we are not talking about rational human beings. If we look at the behaviour of these human beings, I guess it is an easy conclusion to reach. Their behaviour in putting the bill before us indicates they have not acted in a rational manner; therefore, one may conclude they are not rational.

Canada Oil and Gas Act
We shall go one step further. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his successor will be faced with dilemmas. There will be pressures on the part of Canadian people, in any kind of energy crunch, to move forward and produce the oil or the energy we need. If the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources proceeds in that fashion, and if in fact we are in any kind of crisis, then the pressure will be tremendous.
In those circumstances, in view of the political heat which can be generated in this House and the pressure which can be brought to bear on ministers by grass roots organizations, will that minister have, as his or her number one priority, the intention to protect our environment, or will he or she be more likely to proceed and to say "To heck with the environment; we are going to produce the oil". I suggest that nine times out of ten the minister will say "Produce the oil and to heck with the environment."
That is why I think the amendment which would make the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) responsible for environmental issues, whether they occur north of 60 or south of 60, is one which members of this House must support. If we reach beyond this House to people who may be watching the proceedings this afternoon, may we say to them that they have a responsibility to get in touch with a minister of the Crown, or with the Prime Minister, and express their concerns about a piece of legislation which has environmental provisions in it that will clearly be forgotten, subverted, or ignored? This piece of legislation is the responsibility of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources or the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Their greater responsibility to the people of Canada lies in the direction of production and development. They are not the watchdogs of our environment. They do not have the background and they will not have the primary mandate which would allow them to do the kind of job Canadians have a right to expect from their government.
As I said in the beginning, environmental issues are generally not the most compelling issues for Canadians on a day-today basis. If we pollute our fresh water supplies and continue to pollute our air, the long-term consequences for all of us are horrible to contemplate. In an age such as the one we are now in, with the complexity of our industrial growth and development, surely we in the House of Commons can fund and mandate a ministry with the sole major preoccupation of protecting the environment. When we create an environmental ministry to protect us over the longer term, surely we should look at every piece of legislation which involves the environment and has provisions related to the environment. We should say absolutely that the responsibility for enforcement and for allocating the necessary dollars to conduct the studies to protect us should reside in that one department of government with a total mandate and advocacy stance within cabinet and the House dedicated to the long-term protection of the health of Canadians through environmental protection.
It is inconceivable to me that party discipline and party loyalty could ever be called upon in the House to back a
provision in a bill which has such long-range potentially negative consequences for the health and well-being of Canadians. There are times, places and issues which should take us beyond the hurly-burly of daily politics, beyond the rigidity of party power. In that category of events is the issue of the environment. In its simplest terms, it is clean air and clean water and their protection over time.
There are other problems. There is a general lack of clarity from time to time. I see my time has run out, but in conclusion I say that all of us in the chamber have a responsibility, in terms of this piece of legislation, to back the proposed amendments which would protect us in the future.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I speak on this particular piece of legislation and the environmental resolutions before us. It is important to recognize that this is not a good piece of legislation. People have said that it is immoral in terms of its orientation toward the rip-off of resources. People have said that it allows too much discretion on the part of the minister and that it sets up conflicts of interest between development for Indian people and environmental issues. By and large, all of this is true. There has been a reluctance to place in the legislation guidelines under which we would like to see oil and gas developed. The entire bill is extremely vague. It does not provide any security for Canadians as a whole, particularly native people. Indeed it will create some very questionable situations in terms of the environment.
I am pleased to see a former minister of Indian affairs in the House. I should like to address some of the specific predicaments this legislation will create for the native people and communities in an area defined by the government as Canada lands, the area off the coast of British Columbia.
It just so happens that a very determined and active band council from the community of Waglisla on the coast of British Columbia about 300 miles north of Vancouver is in Ottawa for today and next week. They are very concerned about Bill C-48. I hope some of the recommendations in my speech which have also been put forward by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) will be adopted by the government and acted upon.
I am sorry that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) is not able to be here. I listened with a great deal of attention to his presentation. I was under the impression he was to be in Toronto today and not in the House. The band which is here presently has been trying repeatedly to meet with the minister. Hopefully in the next day or two that meeting will be forthcoming. It is very difficult for people in the north or in the far west of this country to plan adequately and to follow up on commitments if they cannot meet with ministers and officials to discuss their plans and obtain basic information on how such legislation will affect them. We are asking those communities to bear all the risks. They will take all the risks while the oil companies of the urbanized areas of central Canada will move in, rip-off the resource and leave.
October 19, 1981

I should like to run through some of the areas which will be affected by this bill. There is the community of Bella Bella and the band council which is in Ottawa today. Also there is Bella Coola, which is an interesting place. It is where Alexander Mackenzie, the first Canadian to cross the country, landed. As a matter of fact, the ancestors of the present band were there to meet him. The attention of the government has not really developed beyond the attention which was given to it by Alexander Mackenzie. The only level of development in that community is the struggle of those people in planning.
Another native community in my riding is at Gold River, the Mowachaht band. They have a small settlement at Friendly Cove and another one at Tahsis. One of the individuals there, an Ambrose Maquinna, happens to be a direct descendant of the Maquinna who met Captain Cook at Friendly Cove several hundred years ago. He is also a hereditary chief of the group. That was the beginning of the bad times, and it has become worse under the Liberals. Let us cook the Liberals.
There is Klemtu, a community in which the government allowed the shutting down of a cannery. It meant instant unemployment for the whole native community. For two decades the community has been struggling to get rolling again. Government bureaucrats travel in and out of that community on chartered aircraft; there is no problem. But the people who live in Klemtu and want to go to the hospital must pay $233 for a charter flight to go 35 miles in order to connect with a flight to Vancouver. Their children were unable to come home from school one particular Christmas because the British Columbia government refused to put in a ferry. That is the responsibility of the federal government. It contributed $9 million to improve coastal transportation and told British Columbia to go it alone. We are not imposing any criteria, and the people of Klemtu suffer. They pay anywhere from three times to ten times the price we pay for food in stores, if they can get it and if it is in a fit condition to eat. Percy Star, the chief of Klemtu, has been struggling for years. They were supplied with electricity a little while ago. They have been working on that project since 1923.
The Kitasoo band has been struggling against a government that does not really care and does not really know where they live.
Oweekano is another beautiful example. In the community of Oweekano the electrical plant broke down and it was without electricity for eight months. I should like to see what would happen if the city of Ottawa was without electricity for eight months. Perhaps the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) could make the government move faster to fulfil its responsibilities. At the present time the generators in Oweekano are ready to break down again and still there is no help from the government. The community wrote to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development but did not receive any acknowledgement of its correspondence. The government has cancelled a memorandum of agreement and its financial contract with this community.

The Tsulquate is another major example of government neglect. One could ask members in every row of the government benches and not find one person who knows where Tsulquate is or the conditions in which the people there live. Yet the councils and the people of these communities are dedicated and are pushing ahead, but without resources.
The Fort Rupert is an advanced band which lives in an ideal location. The band is making progress but certainly not as much as it would like to and could. If the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the government would assist it instead of handicapping it, it would make tremendous progress.
In Queen's Cove and Nuchatlitz, which is the home of the Ehattesaht band, the same thing is happening. When the last round of oil drilling occurred on the west coast of Vancouver Island, there was virtually a blowout off Tofino. If we should get a blowout there, it is not the people of Ottawa or of central Canada or Vancouver who will suffer the consequences, it is the Ehattesaht band, the communities of Nuchatlitz and Queen's Cove that will be covered in oil.
This group of people is experiencing tremendous problems with development. Unemployment ranges from 70 per cent in good times to 100 per cent in off seasons. Most of the communities have enormous unemployment. The government does not even know that they exist. The organization set up by the government confounds development, thwarts planning, withholds resources and unnecessarily complicates their lives. They have never had a land claim settlement. That is their hereditary land. Cook and Mackenzie came along and brought the civilization of the white man which only made things worse. By and large, through this legislation I think we have to begin to orient our thinking to the plight of the native communities.
Today their representatives come here for information. They would like to know what is going on and how they might be invited to participate. They have questions about how their land claims will be dealt with. This is an extremely important question because the people who will benefit from the development will be those in the oil companies and the urbanized areas of Canada. If we should get a blowout off the Queen Charlotte Sound like the Ixtoc blowout, Owikeno Lake would fill with oil and on the whole coast of British Columbia-the marine culture and fishing industry would be destroyed. The total burden of the risk would fall heavily on these communities.
In terms of environmental enhancement, social enhancement and the benefits of economic participation, I suggest the government should insist that oil companies working in the area and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources begin a dialogue with the people and give them information about what will happen. They should also make funds available so that the people can hire the necessary consultants and experts and then plan for and participate in whatever opportunities become available.
I would also urge that the government move forward with the land claim issue so that the people can participate in this

October 19, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
matter and share in the resources. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and other ministers have told us what a great bill of goods this bill is and I am sure they would want the Indian people from the west coast of British Columbia and, indeed, all Indian people to share in those resources and not be ripped off and forgotten.
There are other communities on northern Vancouver Island that are affected, such as Port Hardy, Port Alice on the west coast, Port McNeill, Alert Bay and Sointula. These communities have been isolated for years. They are basically single industry towns where the men work in the community but young people have nothing to do. For years they have been deprived of the social amenities available in large urban areas. Many people say that if they do not like it they should go back there. But, Mr. Speaker, these communities supply the raw materials which give other people in this country jobs in manufacturing industries and provide the social amenities they enjoy. Yet these are the people who are forgotten, although it would not take much effort to go to them and see what faces them.
All of a sudden, there are indications of interest. You can see the sharks moving in the pool already. They know that there will be action so the speculators and promoters are trying to take up options and nail down the opportunity to make money. They are interested in land development and are slightly ahead of the local planning efforts in the communities. As a result, the cream is skimmed off and hauled away. The same thing has happened in Norway, Scotland and to some degree in Newfoundland where governments have been late with the basic planning.
If this legislation is to pass, I urge the government to inform the communities about what will happen to them, and to provide funding so that the communities can hire consultants and expert planners to assist them. This is necessary so that communities are not ripped off and high-graded by the professional speculators in this country and in the United States who derive enormous wealth from taking advantage of the small communities that do not have access to funding and expert planning.
By the time they become aware of what will happen in their area, there is not much they can do. The plans have been made and the local people left out, although it is they who will ultimately bear the expense of development. Perhaps the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources could send people into the communities to tell the local councils, the regional boards and the band councils what is going on. They could indicate whether they would be able to participate in the planning.
In my area there are 15 municipalities, five regional boards and 17 native communities that do not know whether they will even be given information or whether they can participate. The federal government should make money available to those communities so that they can begin taking part in planning now. There seems to be about a two-year lead time. That is a godsend because it gives time for adequate planning. If the communities are aware of the effect this legislation may have
on them, then they will have time to make plans and prevent the bad experiences which have occurred in other areas from occurring here.
I urge the government to make that information available to the people involved. Funds should also be made available. Compared to the tremendous royalties that the government will rake in, the funds required for planning would be but a drop in the bucket and would be of tremendous help to the communities.
In talking about development on the west coast of British Columbia, I should like to take up my favourite topic, the coastguard. I see a colleague opposite from the committee grinning. I suppose he is wondering what the coastguard has to do with exploration for oil and gas in British Columbia. I would ask him to cast his mind back to the Ixtoc incident when it took nine months to cap the oil leak into the Gulf of Mexico. That area does not have the handicaps of the west coast such as terrible weather, reefs, islands, fog and, generally, difficult marine and air navigation. The coastguard would be a tremendous help in that area. I have checked with the coastguard and apparently there is nothing in their five-year plan which deals with offshore drilling on the central coast of British Columbia. There is no vessel traffic management system for the central coast so that ships will not pile into each other or run aground as they did in Alert Bay and other places. Numerous vessels have gone down but no search and rescue unit is available.
Referring to the communications system, let me just use this little example. There is a little native community on the west coast called Kyuquot. I forgot about that in my rundown. All the fishermen are exposed to the areas which could blow out. There is a weather system there. The fishermen leave at four in the morning to go fishing; they listen to the weather forecast the night before, if that is all they can get over the transcribed broadcasts, which states that the winds are light and variable and that all is well. They sail out at about 4.30 in the morning; and when they are out about 20 or 30 miles, all of a sudden it is blowing 70, out in the open Pacific. The next stop from Kyoquot is Japan. It is a really interesting time.
A couple of towing companies just recently lost barges there. They were getting their weather forecasts from the night before, which were the only forecasts available on the transcribed broadcasts. They got out there, the winds were blowing very strongly and they lost their barges which were full of goods. I wonder that the insurance companies do not sue the Government of Canada for failing to provide adequate weather forecasts. The Government of Canada cancelled the weather ships. We need good forecasting there. However, at least as far as I can understand, the coastguard is asleep at the switch. We need vessel traffic management and search and rescue facilities there. We need environmental protection against an oil spill close to the Port Hardy area or the central coast area so that if drilling goes badly and if, in fact, a decision is made to accept those risks, at least we can move quickly, capitalizing
October 19, 1981

on the experience of others, to protect that very delicate and very difficult area.
Navigation in that area is always a hazard, especially in winter. I hate to travel in that part of the country. I literally fear for my life in the wintertime, and experience shows that that is probably a legitimate fear. Yet these people want to go and drill for oil and gas in an earthquake zone. The last time we had a severe accident out there, it took ten days to find six people who went down in a Beaver. That falls pretty well squarely on the government. The government would have found them in one and one half hours if there had been a functioning ELT on the aircraft, and that strikes very close to home.
We need that coastguard attention to that area. We need development in that area for the protection of the people who live there. This government has an obligation to provide some protection against the tremendous risks that it is asking the residents of that area to bear. It has an obligation to tell them what is happening. It has an obligation to put forward funds. The province of British Columbia and the Government of Canada should be putting up funds so that those communities can develop effective community plans so that they are not ripped off by the class of speculators who are already in those communities, buying up land and promoting opportunities which will enhance themselves rather than the community. I think it is vitally important that some very serious attention be paid to that matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking today about Bill C-48, which is an incredibly complex bill. There are virtually hundreds of sections and subsections, when they are all added together, which will affect huge areas of land on the west coast, in the north and in the east. The bill has gone through first and second reading. It went into committee, where virtually dozens of witnesses appeared. Hon. members on all sides of the House spent a great deal of time considering the various powers and authorities, and conflicts of interest which arose, and have now proposed a number of amendments. Right now we are debating some seven amendments dealing with the environment.
I think the important thing to recognize is that none of the amendments to this bill and motions for amendment which are now before the House is spurious or anything like that, whether put forward by the official opposition or the NDP. These are amendments about which people have talked for many hours, and regarding which we have heard the evidence. We have heard from the experts who came from all across the country and from all of the various interest groups, and they have proposed a series of amendments which are now before the House.
My first point is that it is a major disappointment to me that the government does not accept more of these amendments which, as I say, are reasonable in every respect. I would urge the government to accept them and I do not know why it would not. It is a bit similar to the constitutional committee, where virtually dozens of amendments put forth were perfectly good amendments and would have improved that bill for the people of Canada; yet the government accepted only its own amendments from its own members. A couple of amendments from our side and maybe one or two from the NDP were accepted, more by way of tokenism than as a real acceptance of amendments which would have improved the bill.

smacks of retaining colonial status, which I believe is unacceptable to the west. Fortunately, in Alberta we have control over our resources but it took a huge battle to win that control. A provincial Liberal government fought from 1905 to 1921 for the resources but failed. It took the United Farmers Association who fought from 1921 to 1930 to secure resource control. So for 25 years the people of Alberta, while residents of a province, did not have control over their resources. Those resources were controlled by Ottawa. It was only when that control got into the hands of the provincial politicians, who were closer to the people, that decisions on development were made protecting not only the investment climate but the environment as well.
I believe that is exactly the case with the north. People making the decisions concerning the environment, the rate of development and where lines should go, should not be a distant group of people in Ottawa, however well intentioned they may be. There is no doubt that our civil servants are highly trained and skilled, but by virtue of being in this fairyland, on the hill in Ottawa, they have no idea how people actually live and work out in the field. I believe people out in the field can make far better decisions. We will still have oil development, there is no doubt about that because they want it. But when the native and Inuit communities come up with a package giving a rate of development that will be in their best interests as well as everyone else's, surely the focus of that decision should be with them and not on a distant Ottawa.
One thing westerners have learned over 75 years is that decisions to be made will be made on a political basis. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) said that he and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources can work together, that they will work together and that they have created a committee, presumably of experts, who will make decisions. However, if there is a dispute between the two departments, who will solve that dispute? In other words, which ministry will make the decision? Depending upon which department makes the decision, what will the basis of that decision be? From where I stand, coming from the west, there is no doubt that the politics of the situation will rule. In other words, the people of southern Canada, who elect more members into this House, will make a decision in their best interests rather than in the interests of the three or four members of Parliament who represent the north.
Why would the courts not be authorized to make that decision? Better yet, why would the government not have an independent ombudsman who could make those decisions? Decisions would then be made out in the open after a hearing rather than being made behind the closed doors of the government in power, whichever government that may be.
I was amazed when I looked at the bill to see that there was no statutory authority at all for the creation of a committee to make these types of decisions. What is the authority for this committee that has been set up? It will clearly add a bureaucracy which will in turn add enormous cost and create an enormous time delay.

My colleague said it would be by convention. I am not all that impressed with the government's upholding of convention.
A major point of conflict will be between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who, under this bill, has far too much responsibility, and the environment minister. At the very least I would encourage the government to make it crystal clear that the final decision should be made by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). In his day-to-day contacts with people across this country, he will be meeting citizens who care for the troposphere and the continuation of mankind beyond the next 25 years, certainly beyond the next election.
I would like to go through some of the sections that have been amended. Motion No. 4 is a good proposal. This motion would define spills. Surely to goodness when a government brings a bill before the people of the country setting up all sorts of serious offences, particularly if individuals are involved, a clear definition of its terms should be spelled out so that people and corporations can decide what is or is not a breach. We have no definition of what is a spill in this bill. One of the motions is to call that definition. Surely that is a motion that could be accepted. If there is no definition, the courts will ultimately decide and that involves an enormous time delay and enormous cost. As different types of spills occur, reference will have to be made to the courts again and again.
Motion No. 51 would remove any distinction between an unauthorized and an authorized spill. Surely that is an area of incredible silliness on the part of the government. It is putting clauses in the bill which sort of say that if you authorize a spill, that is fine, and it does not matter how big it is. But if it is unauthorized, however small it might be, you are subject to penalty. That puts a power, again not in the hands of politicians particularly, but in the hands of the bureaucracy. Our common experience with the exercise of bureaucratic discretion is that it invariably becomes arbitrary and unilateral, however well intentioned the individual might be.
Motion No. 53 substantially clarifies the liability of anyone who has violated the environment under the terms of the bill. It does so by specifying that compensation must be paid when pollution impairs, for example, one source of income through loss not only of personal property but also of natural environment. This clearly would be of great interest to the natives in the north and should be accepted instantly by the minister, and for the life of me I do not understand why he does not stand up and do so immediately.
I was disappointed, as were other members, that the Chair disallowed Motion No. 54 proposed by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) on the grounds that it would entail the expenditure of public funds. That amendment was designed to establish a multimillion dollar compensation fund based on

October 19, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
letters of credit from the parties involved in exploration. In the face of damage, compensation to the individual would be awarded through the letter of credit. Surely that would be a worthy motion to be accepted by the government. Again, I have not heard a rational, realistic answer from any of the speakers in the House as to why that amendment was not accepted. There would not be any loss of face for individual Liberal members or the Liberal government. These are proposals designed to make the bill more satisfactory, and so that this nation can continue to go on for many, many years.
In summary, sir, it is most important I believe, first of all, that the conflict of interest between the two ministers be firmly resolved. There should be no doubt about that. Second, there should be this compensation fund that is adequate; and, third, we should have a much more clear definition of how the people in the north are going to be able to ultimately take over responsibility for their resources, just as the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan ultimately took over theirs. What will happen once this bill is firmly entrenched is that it will be virtually impossible for the native community to ever get full provincial status with control of their resources. They simply would not have the numbers of people to do it. It is important for that to be done now and I believe this bill should, indeed, be put off until that occurs.
