Mr. Speaker, there are a good number of issues I would like to address today, one of them being ownership as it relates to my province of Nova Scotia. Unfortunately I will leave that one because I want to take this opportunity to express my views regarding Bill C-48, and to clarify the important role which the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has played and intends to play in the future in the matter of this legislation before the House. This also provides me with the opportunity to show that there is absolutely no foundation for the criticism made by the members of the opposition to the effect that environmental matters are not adequately dealt with under this particular piece of legislation.
I have no quarrel with members opposite who have referred to the great economic importance of the fishing industry to this country and the need to protect and preserve the fishery resource and the environment generally. I can only conclude that their criticisms are based on a misconception of the provisions written into the bill. My intention now, therefore, is to go into some detail to explain to hon. members opposite that the proposed legislation includes various provisions which are sufficient to dispei the fears of those, including myself, who are concerned about the protection of Canada's fisheries and oceans.
For the benefit of this House, I might perhaps point out that under the Department of Fisheries and Oceans Act the duties, powers and functions extended to the minister include the following:
(i)	sea coast and inland fisheries,
(ii)	fishing and recreational harbours,
(iii)	hydrography and marine sciences, and
(iv)	the co-ordination of the policies and programs of the Government of
Canada regarding oceans.
In accordance with these duties, powers and functions, the minister is responsible for the administration of the Fisheries Act, the legislation which governs the management of Canada's fisheries and which dates back to confederation. Neither I nor the minister have to be reminded by members of the opposition that the protection and preservation of the marine environment, including fish and fish habitat, is fundamentally the responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc).
I also wish to point out to members opposite and to remind this House that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is not only entrusted with the protection and management of fisheries, but also has a vital operational and advisory role in terms of the oceanographic and hydrographic aspects of ocean resource development as a whole.
That being so, I am fully aware that exploration for and the eventual production of offshore oil and gas may pose potential hazards to fish resources, to fishing activities and to the marine environment in general. As well, I as a member of Parliament from Atlantic Canada am aware that the offshore oil and gas activities are likely to have a significant impact on the socioeconomic welfare of Canada's coastal and fishing communities.
Both oil and gas, on the one hand, and fisheries, on the other, are resources which are invaluable in terms of Canada's economic future. However, it would be a step backward if the oil and gas resources were allowed to be developed at the cost or to the detriment of the fishing industry. It should be remembered that the life of an oil well is limited to a relatively short economic productive period. The fishery, on the other hand, is a long-term resource that will continue to provide livelihood and food, as it has done for centuries. It is my belief, and one which is shared I am sure by all members of this House, that the oil and gas industry must not unduly interfere with the fishing industry or, indeed, damage it in any way.
In saying that I do not wish to create the impression to my colleagues or to the public at large that I am opposed to offshore oil and gas development. Clearly the oil and gas sector is a major component of the Canadian economy. Oil and gas development must go ahead in a responsible manner; that is to say, in a way which deals adequately with fishing and environmental concerns.
I have said before and I state again that I firmly believe these two industries can coexist in harmony, and I am confident that my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, (Mr. Lalonde), shares this view, as does the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has made a diligent attempt, in my view with successful effort, to ensure the inclusion in this bill of provisions which will adequately serve to protect and safeguard those very concerns which have been expressed by hon. members in this House and by those who appeared before the committee.
October 19, 1981

I believe the need for co-operation and liaison between the departments in this matter is mutually recognized by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In this spirit the two departments have in my view collaborated closely and have united their efforts over the last months to accommodate the matters dealing with fisheries interests raised in representations before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. It is my view and belief that those matters have been duly taken into consideration by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in the latest revision of that particular piece of legislation.
Before I address myself to the specific aspects of this bill, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is also responsible for national programs in oceanography and hydrography. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is carrying out studies and surveys in these two scientific disciplines in the principal area of hydrocarbon exploration and planned production. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is actively involved with the regulatory agencies and with the industry as well as in matters related to the physical hazards to offshore drilling operations of such things as ice and icebergs, ocean currents and waves. The principal objective of this activity by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is to assist in the design and development of safe and efficient offshore structures, and the safe conduct of related shipping operations. In this manner, not only is the Department of Fisheries and Oceans contributing to the economic development of offshore oil and gas, but-and I would emphasize this-it is contributing directly with measures that will help ensure the protection of the marine environment and its living resources. Simply stated, the likelihood or risk of environmental damage is considerably reduced by making sure that every possible safety procedure is built into the offshore operations.
In my view, any scheme devised for the protection and preservation of Canada's fisheries and oceans and the socioeconomic welfare of fishermen and coastal communities must necessarily provide for preventive as well as remedial measures. It is true that all environmental damage cannot be compensated. It is precisely for that reason that preventive measures must be established to minimize the possibility of events which could lead to an environmental disaster. As is often said, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Preventive measures include the entire range of scientific research, risk analysis and contingency planning and so on, while remedial measures include devising fast and effective clean-up methods and providing adequate compensation for any damages that might result.
One provision in the bill deals with the establishment of an environmental studies revolving fund, a proposal which has received the full support of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans from the earliest stages. The proposed fund will then ensure studies required for the assessment of new areas or studies not carried out by proponents or government through
Canada Oil and Gas Act
established responsibilities will be undertaken. It has been agreed that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans will play a vital role in the administration of this fund and in the designation of study areas and requirements.
I should also emphasize that the consultative arrangements between the Departments of Energy, Mines and Resources and Indian Affairs and Northern Development concerning oil and gas development have been in place for a number of years. It is not just yesterday or the day before that they came into place. By means of two senior level committees, the resources management environmental committee and the interdepartmental environment review committee respectively, expert advice is provided on all matters relating to the regulation of oil and gas development. This includes matters such as draft regulations, oil spill contingency plans, approval of leased areas and specific environmental conditions. In addition, scientific information on the marine environment is provided directly on an ongoing basis both to the government agencies concerned and to the fishing industry as a whole.
The bill also proposes the establishment of a new Canada oil and gas lands administration which would bear over-all responsibility for regulation of oil and gas activities on all Canada lands. I have been assured that similar consultative mechanisms to those already in existence will be maintained. In fact, because of the extent of anticipated development in offshore areas, I have been assured by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources before committee and, indeed, in this House, that my concerns respecting fisheries and marine environment will receive particular attention.

Furthermore, the liability provisions include not only damages resulting from spills but also compensation for damages resulting from debris on the ocean floor. The provision is undoubtedly far-reaching in terms of relief for the fishermen, the backbone of the fishing industry, and others who may have their gear damaged by discarded equipment from the oil industry. In this context, Mr. Speaker, I might add that the wide definition of debris which has been incorporated in the bill also came about as a result of an insistence on the part of fishermen, MPs and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
Another significant feature of the liability and compensation scheme is the inclusion of loss of income, including future income in the definition of actual loss or damage. I must emphasize that this provision goes beyond the basis for the award of damages under common law and in my view it is unprecedented in any similar type of legislation. Again, this major improvement was brought about in large part by the efforts of members of Parliament as well as by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
Another feature that is important from my own perspective is the extended limitation period for claims now incorporated in the bill. On the basis of scientific advice from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans it was agreed that the proposed limitation periods should be extended. I am now satisfied that the revised limitations in the new version of the bill are much more realistic in terms of assessing damage or potential damage to the living resources. Furthermore, the compensation scheme under the bill provides for financial responsibility in the form of a letter of credit, a guarantee or indemnity bond. This provision will enable potential claimants such as fishermen to gain access to funds immediately without being
subjected to inherent difficulties often associated with going through the courts. That is a major benefit under this legislation.
I wish to point out that over the years there has been a steady and fruitful exchange of views between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. This consultation process has been reflected in the participation of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in various advisory groups, as I have already pointed out.
However, in the context of this bill co-operation has been further strengthened by the mutual consultations which the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources have had with respect to the many modifications which, I believe, are now found in the bill. I might also add that in some areas there are consultations which involve not only the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources but also the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of the Environment. I think I have quite clearly demonstrated the absence of any foundation for the allegations raised in this House that the environmental provisions of Bill C-48 are inadequate. Indeed, the latest version of the bill, in particular the provisions relating to liability and compensation, in my view reflect the considerable efforts expended by all members of Parliament. I wish to emphasize that hon. members on this side of the House as well as hon. members opposite played a role in bringing that to the attention of both the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I wish to conclude my remarks on this particular aspect of Bill C-48. Mr. Speaker, when one rises to speak about Bill C-48, one feels somewhat like the Arab felt when he entered his harem. He knew what he was there for; he just did not know quite where to begin.
There are many aspects of this bill about which one would want to speak. I will restrict myself to a quick word about what the previous speaker referred to, the role of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc), and address the main part of my remarks in reply to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), who told me I did not have very much patience in listening to his speech. At least I was here to listen to his speech, and I want to reply to it.
With respect to the previous speaker, I suggest to him that he might want to look at the reports of the department to which he referred and specifically the report of Mr. Grinnell, who wrote a report on the implications of offshore petroleum development for Atlantic fisheries, a socioeconomic overview. This was released by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in August, 1981. At page 29 of that report the author says, and I quote:
The U.K. experience tells us that a rapid escalation of petroleum activities can offset routine gains in employment and business activities by losses in environmental values and social conditions, as well as sharp increases in cost of living for those on fixed incomes or in work areas not associated with the petroleum industry-without a commensurate increase in income. In addition, industries competing for labour and space with the new industry, and marketing products in competion with those from industries in low cost situations, may have economic problems. Fishing, if conducted inefficiently, can be particularly vulnerable.
He went on to say why. I just quote that to say that I would not want to see the impression left with fishermen that they will not be vulnerable in many ways to the rapid escalation of oil and gas development about which this bill talks.
1 want to refer to some of the remarks made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources because he gave the impression that everything is hunky-dory, that this bill is fine, that it can proceed and so forth.
With reference to north of 60 the minister has succeeded in doing a strange thing. For the first time in my memory and in the memory of many people he has united the Northwest Territorial government, the Dene and the Indian people in the Northwest Territories, the Metis and the non-status Indians in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon Territorial government, the Indian brotherhood in the Yukon, the non-status people in the Yukon, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and all the Eskimo organizations, business in the north, labour in the north and environmental people in the north. As a matter of fact, everybody in the north opposes this bill, including even the municipalities in the north. He has succeeded in bringing unity to the north in the fact that all oppose this bill. All are united against it.
The question is why. Perhaps it is somewhat of a breakdown in communications or in understanding. This bill sets out a strong regime, in many ways, compared with previous regimes.
I see in the gallery today a representative from the department, specifically Dr. Crosby, who did a very good job in his department working to try to get a hard-hitting regime to-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
gether to deal with the oil industry and other aspects for the first time in a long time. The previous regime was disastrous. However, what has happened with this bill is that in the process the minister, who likes to ram things through, has forgotten to consult in a real way with the northern people. That is very important because they are the ones who have to live with this development.
What the bill does is speed up the development, so the minister should not be surprised when we stand up on behalf of northern native people and other northerners and on behalf of environmental groups and say, "Wait a minute; be careful; fix this bill up, if you can, and see what is happening as a result of this development." It will speed up the pace of development. What else is the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources there for? Its job is to push development. We would not expect these good doctors in the department to do anything else. That is their job. However, we in Parliament, as politicians and as people representing the entire country, must make sure that in putting a bill like this through we protect the interests of certain groups which will be affected by the bill.
This bill has generally been ignored by the press. Look at the press contingent here today. Everybody is interested in the Constitution or in the economy, perhaps, as people should be, but this bill is a real sleeper because it causes some very dramatic effects in the north and offshore. Environmentally speaking, this bill would set a pattern for an environmental regime and for other matters.
When he spoke, the minister gave the impression that the bill would go through easily. Of course it will; it is a question of power. The centre in Canada has the power at the expense of the periphery. That is what the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) meant when he was talking about development overriding the interests of the native people and environmental concerns. Granted, hon. members opposite can do it, but I say to the government that they pay a price. I suggest that the government be prepared to accept motions we present, motions the opposition Conservatives present and, of course, some of its own motions. Even at this stage the government should add amendments to the bill.
In dealing with the bill we in the New Democratic Party have had four main criticisms. The first is that the bill emphasizes Canadianization. We say it is a giveaway because 93 cents of every exploration dollar basically goes toward replacing the big American boys with big Canadian boys. Is that a change? We say no. It will make the Dome Petroleums and the NOVA corporations rich. The Dome Petroleums and the NOVA corporations will rush to drill in the Beaufort Sea and in the north at the expense of the environment.
Second, we have criticized the bill because it overrides the concerns of native people. Liberal members opposite do not have to care, but I put it to them that the Anglican church has informed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that it favours complete withdrawal of the bill. This surely must have some influence. The Roman Catholic bishop Paul Reding read a statement from the Archbishop of Edmonton, Joseph N. Mac-Neil as follows:

October 19, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
I believe this legislation could, in effect, seriously prejudice the settlement of native land claims and further relegate the people of the North to a colonial status within Canada. This issue will have a dramatic influence upon the lives of thousands of our fellow Canadians.
In fact, the minister says this bill is neutral with respect to land claims. You cannot be neutral with respect to land claims. If you are going to develop the north, you have taken all that property off the table in the negotiations. Once again, the native people in the north will become like the native people in southern Canada. They will be the people standing by the road when the trucks roll by; they will be in skid row in Regina or Vancouver instead of taking their proper place in the development of the country. You have to do that by settling land claims first. That is why the matter is there. This bill, as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, may be unconstitutional.
I remind the members that section 34(1) of the Constitution Act says this:
The aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
That principle was accepted in the Constitution. That principle was right. It is a very progressive and ultimately radical principle. The government is to be congratulated on this because it recognizes that the country is made up of the founding peoples, the native peoples, the original peoples, the two other groups, the French and English, and then the multicultural group, the group that came afterwards-that is the genius of the Constitution. It is a wise document. You cannot then come along with Bill C-48 and completely ignore that principle.
Let me now deal with a third criticism of the bill: the environmental aspect. The minister looking over at me said in his speech, "What are you worried about? Dome Petroleum have been drilling. They have drilled hundreds of wells and there has been no spill yet." But, Mr. Speaker, this bill means there is going to be an immense speed up in development. We do not know how to handle offshore spills.
A report in the Ottawa Citizen of May 9, 1981, stated this about a meeting in Resolute Bay, Northwest Territories:
A spokesman for Dome Petroleum Ltd. of Calgary admitted Friday when questioned by concerned Inuit that his company does not have the ability to clean up a major oil spill in the Northwest Passage.
But Ed Pessah told a public hearing that his company, which is proposing a fleet of icebreaking tankers to ship Arctic oil to southern markets, is studying methods to clean up major oil spills and hopes to be able to do that by 1986.
Ed Pessah said:
We probably could not clean up that oil spill today but we are hopeful that we could by 1986. We could not give that guarantee today.
We are here today discussing a bill with inadequate environmental protection, when Dome Petroleum admits, contrary to what the minister told the House, they cannot control an oil spill in the Arctic. What kind of leadership is this? "Have patience," says the minister. The minister should have listened to the remarks made to the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) and the member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) when they talked about specific proposals we made. Why did the minister
not say, "We will accept those proposals. They make sense." For example, we wanted to define an oil spill. I will not go into this in detail, Look at Hansard on page 11796, and you see that the hon. member for Skeena refers to the reasons for defining an oil spill. He talks about cumulative leaks being just as bad as a big spill. That is why you must have a definition of what an oil spill is. He cites the experience in Wales in these words:
Let us look at the experience elsewhere. In Wales, the harbour authority has defined a spill as anything over a few barrels. What this has done is to give a mandate to the local authorities to watch the chronic oil pollution problem closely, but it has also meant that the companies involved have taken the time to train their employees properly and have recognized the importance of controlling these kinds of spills. Incidentally, when a quantified level was set, the spill rate in Wales dropped to one spill in 100 from previous levels.
We advocated that when we brought forward Motion No.
52.	In an excellent speech to the House the other night, the hon. member from Nunatsiaq really dealt with the matter in detail. If you look at what he said, Mr. Speaker, at page 11831 of Hansard, you will find he defined why we want Motion No. 52 of the bill. He dealt with the method of compensating people for spills.
He also dealt with another matter. This is a grave matter. It is dealt with in Motion No. 53. You heard the hon. member from Mississauga also make the point. Bill C-48 would only allow you to go to court over a spill, to sue, or to go to the minister if your property were directly affected. In the north they have walruses and other groups of animals. more detail. However, they should look at it because I believe it is worth while.
The government has made a big mistake with regard to this bill. This is a centralized bill. It is brought down by this government against the wishes and without really consulting the members of the people of the north.
I heard the minister say that in the committee say, "We heard from all kinds of people. We sat for so long. We heard from the government bureaucrats and from the industry. That is who we heard from." We had only one day with the northern people, and the committee refused to go up north. What kind of way is that to run a country like ours? This is a big country. The north is our last frontier. 1 will conclude the substantial part of my speech, Mr. Speaker, by suggesting to the members opposite that they take a look at the amendments we proposed in good faith. It will not cure their bill, but it will help it a bit.
The other point I will make in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that when I was a younger lawyer, I went to a hearing in Inuvik as counsel to the Berger inquiry on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. I did not understand, at first, things about the north. I thought like a southerner and did not understand then the point I just made about collective ownership of animals. I remember the night when Sam Raddi appeared before the inquiry in Inuvik and gave a very quiet speech. Mr. Raddi is blind. He speaks very quietly. He spoke about the time when he was a boy and his father told him that if the animals ever left the Beaufort Sea, the people would go; if the animals go, the people go. It is not just a question of killing polar bears and seals because we in the south may happen to like polar bears and seals. It goes further for northern people. It will kill them if they lose those animals. It will kill their culture. The minister should know better. He should stop this bill. He should go up and consult the people of the north about it. Before third reading, he should try again to talk to the northern people.
We want to keep our northern environment. All parties in the House share this view. We are a northern people. If one reads Canadian literature, one finds over and over again illustrations of how we are northerners. Although we live in southern Canada, we think of ourselves as northern people. There is not a member in the House who does not want to preserve the northern environment. I have been through three or four years of hearings on this matter, and I find that the only way we can preserve the northern environment is by tempering the development of the north, which the minister wants to bring in through Bill C-48 full flight.
It must be tempered with some balances. It must be tempered with a settlement of native land claims and by including all northern people in this bill. In that way we can have both the northern frontier and the northern homeland intact for the people. That is the point we in this corner of the House are making.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party do not have any profound objections to this clause which provides that the minister may appoint an advisory body to advise him with respect to matters relating to the administration of this act and that the governor in council be empowered to pay for their services. In theory, that provision is reasonable. But as we know from experience with the operation of this government in the last few months and years, we know that what is sometimes a reasonable procedure turns out often to be not so reasonable. I do not know that we could find the appropriate language, and indeed it is regrettable that it is even necessary for members of this House to express the hope that this provision be not inserted for the purpose of allowing the minister to reward and remunerate his friends and associates.
It would be nice if we could have some provision in here to ensure that the sleazy behaviour regarding Messrs. Maurice Strong, David Beattie and Joel Bell with respect to the CDC will not be repeated here. It would be nice if we could find the appropriate language to ensure that this particular provision will not be used for some under the table sleazy payments to assistants of the minister. It would be nice if we could find some way to ensure that this provision will not end up as a way for the minister to reward campaign workers, defeated candidates and other loyal Liberals, a habit that has developed with respect to these types of appointments.
Prior to six o'clock today we heard the speech of the former parliamentary secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). He talked about the coming parliamentary reform, perhaps in the new year. One parliamentary reform, which the record of this government indicates is vitally necessary if we are to restore some public respect for this body and for the government, is a reform wherein appointments such as this be made subject to review, so that the remuneration of people who are appointed to advisory boards, boards of directors and various government appointments be made subject to public disclosure and public review. As well perhaps we should assign an advise and consent role to this House, similar to that in the United States. Obviously with a government whose only moral code is the Criminal Code, this kind of unconventional, immoral behaviour is bound to continue. I do not think it does justice to the taxpayers of Canada who ultimately have to pay these salaries.
With the caveat, Mr. Speaker, that some of us in this Parliament at least do find that kind of behaviour by the government sleazy at best, I say on behalf of my party that we have no objection to Amendment No. 5

Mr. Speaker, I suppose than anybody would have to accept the amendment before us as recognition that at some time advisory boards will be used. I wish to point out some of the major concerns of our party and of members of other parties in committee about the role of advisory boards. The legislation should provide for the establishment of specific advisory boards and set out the roles they should play.
I would like to run through what we felt were some of the major shortcomings in this legislation and why advisory boards might be one mechanism which would meet our concerns. The bill leaves tremendous power in the hands of the minister and, as a result, the decisions that affect the lives of Canadians on the west coast, in the north, not the east coast, will be centralized in the hands of the minister.
It is unfortunate that this bill allows for something that we heard complaints about just a few minutes ago, that is, secret dealings. There is a great deal of fear that proper explanations and information will not be available and that opportunity for
input will not occur because of the powerful discretionary role of the minister.
Advisory boards would be of utmost value in overcoming this situation. Such boards should have very specific guidelines dictating their role. The amendment we are considering does not go far enough. There is only provision in the legislation for the appointment of advisory boards. There are no guidelines in the bill and we will only see advisory boards appointed if the minister deems it necessary. He is authorized to pay them but, in my opinion, this legislation should contain guidelines. Advisory boards should be appointed for a specific purpose and guidelines provided. None of this is set out in the legislation before us.
Our party tried to have this included in the legislation, as did the Conservative Party, and some Liberal members tried to get the matter reconsidered. It is unfortunate that the minister and the government did not see the benefit of including it in the legislation.
Bill C-48 is largely an effort to rule by regulation. Other concerned members have expressed the view that the Government of Canada is governing by regulation, by cabinet decision not involving the decisions of the selected representatives and not involving the participation of the people.
By governing by centralized power and by a very centralized bureaucracy, I hope the government will realize it is losing touch with the people, that it no longer has relevance. It is very concerned about its image and about federal input into projects. It is a big concern for them, and we see that by the advertising budgets they use in trying to get at that problem.
The real dilemma is that the government has left the people. It sits here in Ottawa and makes decisions about over-all budgets, but in the rural areas of Canada the federal government is an obstacle to the way of life. There rural Canadians can no longer relate to their government. During the past week there was a small group of people here trying to see a cabinet minister, trying to talk to someone who affects their lives. They had a difficult time even getting an appointment. Some ministers are open and make a tremendous effort to see these people but others keep their doors locked, both here and in regional and district offices. The right to make decisions in the community has been removed totally. The right to provide meaningful input into the decision-making process has been virtually denied. The whole concept of centralizing the bureaucracy and governing by regulation has created great havoc in this country. Advisory boards which would represent major interests would go a long way to making Bill C-48 more palatable and more meaningful to people at the local level.
I question the goals contained in this bill. It has been said here that this legislation will not, in the final analysis, meet the needs of Canadians. We will be pouring enormous amounts of money into megaprojects that will just create enormous profits for the oil companies. There is great fear that those megaprojects will draw money out of Canada.
We have been assured by the minister that his intentions are honourable. His goals may not be clear, but certainly they are

there to benefit Canadians. But he will not put those guidelines in the bill, he will not include anything that Canadians can hook onto. We fought tooth and nail to get an advisory board on industrial benefits that would bring together industry, labour and government into a forum that would meet regularly to exchange information. Many people in industry wanted to get involved but had no idea what was going on. Labour, a major component of the Canadian economy, consulted individually, but there was a real need for a solid advisory board to ensure that industrial benefits came into Canada. The minister refused to accept the concept.
The measure before us goes a small distance toward allowing that advisory boards could be appointed, but we need those guidelines spelled out. We should set up advisory boards to provide meaningful input into government so that the decisions they make are relevant to people who live in Newfoundland, B.C., or Nunatsiaq. These advisory boards are absolutely critical. They would involve local people in decision making and give them a sense of participation in government.
Unfortunately, members of the government have been pushed east of the Red River. If things keep going as they are, we will see them pushed right out the other end. People do not see the reason for the decisions which have been made by the bureaucracy, nor do they find them helpful. I know this is not the intention of hon. members opposite. I have talked to them about these problems. They are aware of them and are sympathetic but somehow there is slippage and when these decisions are made, people do not identify with them. The people do not identify with the goals that are set, nor with the decisions that are made. They really resent the removal of decision making from their communities.
There is still a chance that we can deal with significant amendments and include the question of advisory boards. I think it would serve the government well in terms of its longterm interest. It would certainly be of great benefit to the people in Canada living in small communities which stand to be affected by this legislation.
I would like to say a few words about patronage, too, because it is a very interesting subject. I suppose the intended goal of patronage is to reward people who have served an organization for a long time or who have been influential and helpful and to have a political ally on those boards. Governments often do not have to worry about defection or anything else. One tries somehow to balance the question of qualification and patronage. However, there is a reaction in the community. I point to Spadina as one of the things we all look on as a colossal blunder in terms of patronage. What was the justification for removing the elected representative? I suppose in the final analysis it was a victory for democracy, which I have heard some hon. members suggest.

I have difficulty knowing why we would debate the two motions together. I do not see the relevance between the two motions. I will now speak to my motion.
What I am proposing in this amendment to Bill C-48 is to make it clear in the law that frontier lands, Canada lands on which oil and gas discoveries are made, are not exempt from native land claims. Many have said that under certain amendments contained in the bill this is done. Given the non-definition of aboriginal claims, I suggest it is not distinctly clear that Bill C-48 would cover any lands subject to claim by native people, given that certain discoveries are made on those lands. Native people have reason to question the government's good faith with respect to land claims. They question this because of the government's record. The claims in the north have proceeded very slowly. I can look at the Dene land claims and the COPE agreement as an example of this. They have been working on these agreements for a number of years. They are really no further advanced as far as the settlement is concerned.
Then we look at the first modern land claim agreement, the James Bay and Northern Quebec agreement. As was pointed out in the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development this year, which resulted in an inquiry being conducted by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), that agreement has not been adhered to in good faith. According to the law read by several legal people, perhaps it has been adhered to; but as far as an agreement made in good faith is concerned,
Canada Oil and Gas Act
it has not been. It has affected the health of the native people in the north. Many of the benefits that should have been accrued from moneys that were put aside in that agreement have not come forward.
The natives are justifiably concerned about the future of their aboriginal rights, especially after the constitutional resolution that was proposed. For the first time, aboriginal rights are being defined by the federal government, the provincial government and certain native people who shall be appointed by the federal government. It is understandable that a great deal of concern exists among northern natives about their future, about their unresolved land claims and about the benefits they should receive from the exploration of oil and gas in the north. This is open to question. Bill C-48, if passed, may result in further exploration in those areas.
The aboriginal people of the north are at present gearing up to settle their land claims. At this time, Mr. Speaker, aboriginal title has not been relinquished. The government has, nonetheless, decided to put forward Bill C-48. It is a wide-ranging piece of legislation. Many amendments have already been discussed and some are still in need of discussion. The bill covers virtually every aspect of the oil industry in the north and offshore. In doing so, it will have an enormous impact on the native people of the north.
The other day I was looking at a map of the lands around Great Bear Lake given to Petro-Canada. Those lands are of enormous size. Much of that area is at present open to claim.
Many northern native groups are concerned, justifiably so, that their land claims are in jeopardy owing to Bill C-48. These groups include the Dene, the Inuit, the Council for Yukon Indians and the Metis. They have organized a responsible opposition. Their responsible opposition to the bill was put forward to the standing committee. I was a member of that standing committee. We agreed one day to send members to the northern regions. Most members of this House do not understand the implications of this kind of legislation. The very next day the government rejected travel to the north. Had the members of the committee travelled to the north and allowed themselves even a few days in the north to hear the justifiable reasons for concern from northerners, it would have benefited this House and this country a great deal.
Because the provisions of this bill are to be enacted before the claims in that region are settled, the native people are very concerned that lands subject to claim will be withdrawn from them because of exploration and development. This is a very important concern. That concern has often been brought to me and to other members of this House by way of telegram, by way of hearings before the committee, by telephone and in person. The people in the north seek a voice in developing the lands dealt with in Bill C-48, lands that are under claim by the northern people. They benefit from the resources that exist there. They look forward to this development. They realize that, to a large extent, their economic future depends on the development of the land. They look forward to the jobs that may be created and to the wealth that will adhere to these people, should oil and gas be discovered in that region. There

October 19, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
is also concern about what might happen to their cultural well-being if, as a result of this bill, they lose any rights to the land.
I should like to repeat to the House a statement made by a witness who appeared before the standing committee. I am sorry I do not have the exact quote from the committee's proceedings. He said:
To us, an aboriginal rights settlement represents the means by which we intend to regain control over our own destiny while remaining an integral part of Canadian Confederation. This must mean the ability to influence the pace and direction of development in our region so that our institutions and values are not overridden by rapid resource exploitation. It means equally some measure of access to the revenues which will accrue from developments which take place on our lands. It means also the right to determine the kind of developments which take place on our lands and to prevent adverse impacts on the peoples and the environment of the North from oil and gas developments.
I suppose that statement says it all. First, it indicates a concern about the pace of development and how it affects claims. Second, it indicates a desire to participate in some of the wealth, a matter which is not addressed in the bill. No trust funds have been set up to allow native peoples to move forward politically and economically and thus benefit from any oil and gas which may be taken from this region. Surely that should be a concern of government and of members of Parliament. The only basis for development which the north has at the present time is the resources which may be taken from those lands. This was said before the committee by the witness. Third, he indicated that northerners want to determine the pace of development to some extent, which is one of the reasons why members have brought up the need for advisory boards. Because there is a complete lack of assurance in this legislation that these people will have any influence over the resource development of the lands of the north, and because they fear this will not be negotiable once development is begun, native groups are understandably deeply concerned by the implications of Bill C-48.
I recall that the COPE negotiations were going on, oil and gas exploration in the Beaufort Sea was allowed, and immediately these lands were withdrawn from negotiation by government negotiators. Perhaps there was no legitimate claim, but at the same time it was an example of the reason for the great concern about this legislation in the north.
There is also a feeling among native groups that Bill C-48 makes a mockery of so-called aboriginal rights contained in the proposed Charter of Rights. By virtually ignoring aboriginal title, the bill would seem to deny its existence despite the support given it in the charter, even though the definition clause is open to a great deal of question by native peoples.
The conflict is obvious and is clearly a cause for concern. It is because of the concerns of native peoples that I have put forth Motion No. 6. While it is true that nothing in the bill indicates that the drilling of oil or gas wells means that the land is ineligible for claims or settlements, problems may well arise. I have given some reason for that in referring to the COPE agreement and its development. The concern is there. This is why I believe we should put something positive in the
bill so that native people need not fear the removal of certain lands due to the striking or finding of oil or natural gas. The activity occurring afterward will necessarily involve interests competing with those of native peoples, so a claim will be much more difficult to settle. Such land might be deemed ineligible for the negotiation process. Harry Daniels of the Native Council of Canada before the committee said:
Once the drill rigs are up and production centres on the drawing boards and approved by government, there will be no turning back. Do you really think that under these circumstances the government would withdraw these lands?
The amendment I propose is a simple one. It reads:
No land or oil or gas interests relating thereto shall be withdrawn or withheld from negotiation in the settlement of any claim, right, title or interest for any reason other than the creation of a national park in which all natural resource development is prohibited.
I believe this type of protection is essential. It means more than any other amendment which has been proposed so far by the government for the protection of native peoples and their claims in the next few years. It is essential to entrench in this bill the right of natives to negotiate in respect of any land to which they believe they have a claim, regardless of its resource potential. This amendment is put forward in good faith, to protect legitimate land claims. Certainly I hope the government will consider that it has some merit and add it to the bill as it now stands.

How can we have development of the north, go ahead with physical development, and be neutral toward a claim over the physical environment, the pace of development, the social impact, and all these kinds of things? The Conservative party attacked this bill by indicating that it gives the minister too much discretion. If the hon. member looks at it, he will see that the minister's discretion is very rigid. We looked at this as we tried in committee to make the bill more neutral to native claims.
First I should like to indicate why we wanted to make it neutral toward native claims. On this side of the House we are convinced that settling the native land claims is the only way that we can begin to give native people their rightful place in this country so that they may become real partners in this development. They should not be left out of this bill.
You will recall that when I spoke this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned a native person standing at the side of the road and a truck going by. That is the image or the symbol of past development in this country, and I know that the hon. member opposite wants things to be different.
I should like to elaborate on what I mean about the discretion being rigid. There is provision in the bill that the minister can deal with the Crown's share. He can give it to a government organization like Petro-Canada but he cannot give it to a native development corporation, an aboriginal corporation or a local corporation in the north. There is no such provision in the bill.
I have said before that the bill is not neutral and I want to say something more about that. There will be physical development but that is not neutral. As development is speeded up, it will have an effect on the environment and that is not neutral. It changes things; it has an effect. There will be social impact as development advances and that is not neutral; it has an effect. To say that the bill is neutral is just absurd on that physical level. For example, there is no mention in the bill of giving the native people any part of the royalties, nor is there any mention of giving them equity in the development. There is no mention of giving native people or the northern territorial governments any rights of revenue sharing. If the territories are to become provinces and we would like to see that, and if they are going to take their place in Canadian confederation-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us tonight is a very important one. It sets out the regulatory aspects, guidelines or game plan for the oil and gas exploration and development in the north. Certainly what happens in the north will have a significant impact on the future of our country.
I am concerned about the bill in its present form because I really believe it lacks several serious and important elements, one of which is consideration of the impact it will have upon the environment. I spoke on that matter briefly the other night and it has been debated to a certain extent today.
I am also concerned that the bill fails to adequately consider the impact that oil and gas activity will have on people who live on the Canada lands, because it fails to consider the rights of the native peoples who have lived on those lands for generations. As it stands, the bill does not make provision for the aboriginal rights of the native people to dwell on those Canada lands north of the 60th parallel. There is no reference in the bill to claims that might be negotiated after it is enacted, and I think that could be a very dangerous omission. The land claims that exist today are far from being settled; in fact, for some native people the process has just begun. The government did not see fit, however, to include a provision in

October 19, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
the bill to protect the claims of the native people. We may wonder why those provisions were not made and we may doubt whether the government has any real concern for the native people who live on the Canada lands.
As the bill reads at present, only claims settled prior to the enactment of this legislation would be protected, but obviously, Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. We must have some form of written guarantee that lands under development would not be left out of any future negotiations. Although there is nothing in the bill that exempts developing lands from land claim negotiations, it is unlikely that the federal government would be willing to negotiate when the drilling rigs are actually in operation and when matters have proceeded from the drawing board to the oil patch.
The government has not demonstrated, so far, that it is willing to consider negotiations on the land claims. I think that gives us reason to believe that once the activity has begun in the north, it is unlikely that the government would be willing to listen. We can see that it has very little concern for native problems and it will be less likely to listen when activity has come to a head than it is now.
Motion No. 6 which has been placed before us by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) is very specific and important. It begins to deal directly with the problems created by the bill before us. I should like to read the motion into the record again because it is important and deals with the problems that we may face. The relevant part of the motion reads as follows:
No land or oil or gas interests relating thereto shall be withdrawn or withheld from negotiation in the settlement of any claim, right, title or interest for any reason other than the creation of a national park in which all natural resource development is prohibited.
This means that the concerns of the native people will not be pushed aside and forgotten once exploration has begun. Lands that are under development will not be exempt from any negotiations for aboriginal rights.
I firmly believe that this amendment must be included in the bill, Mr. Speaker. The guarantee for the protection of native rights must be provided and there must be a guarantee that the natives will have an opportunity to pursue a fair and just settlement of their aboriginal rights. Without this amendment and the guarantee, I really believe that native claims will be prejudiced. This is particularly important now when we are at such a crucial point in the negotiation of land claims.
Up to date, negotiations with the government have proceeded very slowly; in fact, negotiations are, to a large part, not yet under way. For example, if we look at the Mackenzie Valley, we find that the federal government has not yet even named a negotiator to continue negotiations in that area. It is clear that they would rather see the possibility of further negotiations, just tossed out the window. Last year, the government finally began to look at settlements on part of the land, the lands that we are discussing tonight; but, again, we see a bit of a dirty pool game going on there, because as negotiations were beginning, so were the hearings on the application to build the Norman Wells pipeline. Does that sound like fair play? Does it sound like an earnest attempt to settle outstanding land claims?
It is no wonder that natives fear for their future and for the future of their children, because this bill does not give an indication that the government remembers them or that it considers their rights. It just seems to clearly demonstrate the lack of concern of the government for our native people. That lack of concern of the government is not new. In fact, back in 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
I think that all of us feel a sense of guilt, not so much toward the Indian as toward the fact that we have not addressed our minds to this problem.
That was 12 years ago; and in 12 years, the government has not seriously or genuinely addressed these concerns. Is it not now time to address it? If the Prime Minister was really feeling that guilt 12 years ago, then why are we not seeing some action taken now, if not in the past 12 years? I do not think we can afford to ignore these concerns any longer, because native concerns are not like some problems; they will not simply disappear. They will not disappear until native rights on Canada lands have been settled. That problem will not go away. We should not let the government just push them out of the way and push them out of our areas of concern.
Through history, there have really been very few assurances that the government is concerned about these problems. These people have always been pushed around. They have always felt as though their rights have been ignored. Then, suddenly, a little while ago, along came the Constitution and the Charter of Rights including, in particular, the entrenchment of native rights. Suddenly it seemed as though there were some kind of a positive step, because the government was finally willing to notice these concerns and it was finally willing to stop ignoring our natives.
Then along came Bill C-48. All of a sudden we had a mockery of that whole Charter of Rights. We see that the intentions there were, in fact, very hollow. The principles of Bill C-48 run exactly contrary to the principles which were outlined in that charter. In fact, the bill goes even further than that, and contradicts the principles which were laid out in the National Energy Program. The National Energy Program indicated concern with the impact of resource development on native peoples and northern Canadians. I would just like to refer to one particular part of that program. It reads:
There will have to be assurances that the interests of the residents of this region are protected, and that they have the opportunity to play the role they desire in these activities. The native residents of the region seek-legitimately- more say in the decision affecting energy development, and claim-rightfully- that they should enjoy more of the benefits, and fewer of the costs, from northern resource activity.
It sounds good, but there are an awful lot of hollow words and empty promises, because not very long after the introduction of the National Energy Program, along came Bill C-48 which clearly contradicts the generous and positive sounding claims that we saw in the National Energy Program.
October 19, 1981

So, where are we? What are we to believe? Are we to believe that the government is truly interested in people, such as those we are dealing with here, and their rights, as was apparently demonstrated in the NEP and the Constitution? Or should we, in fact, be paying much more attention to the actions of the government, and a whole lot less attention to its words? I think that Bill C-48 clearly shows us what the government is up to. It clearly shows us that its interest is really in disposing of rights and concerns. It has demonstrated very little interest in aboriginal rights. I doubt whether it has ever had any real interest or whether it will ever have any real interest in the end. A Toronto columnist, Mr. J. B. McGeachy, had this to say about the matter:
We sing about the north, but we live as far south as possible.
Coming from a part of Canada which is in the north, that is a familiar tune to me, and it is one that I can clearly identify with. This government does sing about the north. It sings about the resource potential, and it sings about development which is possible in these vast lands; but, as this columnist has pointed out, it somehow wants to stay in the southern part of Canada. It only wants to reap the benefits. It does not ever want to set foot on these northern lands.
When we were dealing with this bill in committee, it was proposed that we visit the north; in other words, that we go into this area to discuss with the native and aboriginal people their concerns on their own home base. The government was not interested in that and, as a result, we ended up not going north.
The reversal of that decision really exposes the raw bone of blatant disregard for native concerns that we have seen from this government. It has demonstrated no concern for the people, no concern for their culture, and no concern for the political development of the north. The only interest which seems to be demonstrated is to take as much as possible without giving anything in return. I wonder if it is any wonder that the natives do have a fear for their future. I wonder if it is any wonder that they do mistrust the government, a government which seems to rule from an armchair, thousands of miles away from the problems and from the reality of the situation.
The native people have a real and just cause for fearing exploitation because they have been exploited and they have been given the raw end of the deal. I think that all of us have tasted the bitterness of exploitation. We have all known, to some extent, the feelings arising from rights being taken away when we were too helpless to fight back. These particular people have tasted that bitterness of generations. For generations, they have known the government as an agency which is far away, an agency which knows little about the real problems, and an agency which does not care and which cannot be trusted.
I think that all of us would like to believe that we live in some sort of an enlightened nation, one which operates under democratic principles, where people are equal, and where all people are given the same basic chance. However, when we look at this bill, we find that it is nothing more than an
Canada Oil and Gas Act
illusion. We really begin to see the true intentions of the government because it continues to exploit these people, it continues to ignore their concerns, and it continues to infringe upon their rights.
People of the north have been subjugated to the status of a colony for a long time. By enacting this particular piece of legislation, we only confirm that status. The irony of that whole process is that we are now hearing lots of talk about bringing home our Constitution from Britain to erase any hint of colonialism from our relationship with the United Kingdom or with Britain. The irony is that while we are erasing the colonialism from the past, we are confirming it in the present and entrenching it in our future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate by commenting on this area of concern. I have read the provision which the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Schellenberger) has carefully put forward. Very clearly, the principle put forward is completely acceptable. It is a questionable practice to allow the exploitation of resources to go ahead before dealing with the fundamental issue of who owns the land. Maybe the problem is with the drafting. As the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) has said, there is a problem in drafting the legislation. But whatever it is, the key point is the principle. That principle was hammered home time and time again in committee. The government felt that it had protected the future or the existing interests as more information became available through detailed study. But clearly, nobody except government members accepted that position. Again, it was a discretionary matter. We were told by government members that a clause was included in the bill to ensure that after exploration, after the production facilities have been put in place and after we see what the social and environmental impacts there are, and perhaps even after the resource has been exploited and exhausted, it will still be possible to come back and make a claim. That is rubbish. I cannot find anyone who would accept that concept other than the government. I think the government is fooling itself, but it is not fooling anyone else.
This is very difficult, and there is definitely a misunderstanding, as the parliamentary secretary suggests. But I think the understanding is on the part of the government. There is a desperate need for some action on this particular land claim provision in the bill. We cannot allow alienation before some firm commitments are made. As my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), has said, this bill is not neutral. It does not adequately protect the interests of the native people of Canada in sharing or participating in the development. The establishment of the land claim is extremely difficult.
We talk about the north. There is a lot of activity in the north now. The northern people are trying to work out claims. They are negotiating positions, and so on. But we must also take into account the west coast where things are very different.
The native people who live on the west coast are at various stages of development. Some very sophisticated bands have worked out land claims. They have attempted to define their interest in the lands on the west coast and have presented it to
the government. The process is moving very slowly, whereas the development of oil and gas offshore on the west coast is moving much faster. The technology is in place. Procedures will evolve much more quickly than the native people can deal with it, unless the government specifies in the legislation exactly what it is going to do to protect their interests.
The west coast is unique. The native people who live there have an interest in the land and the sea from which they try to make a living. Most people there are committed to living on government welfare. They do not like it. They have been alienated from their land already. I would have a hard time expressing it better than the previous speaker who suggested that for 200 years we have inflicted a totally colonial regime on the native people, and that this particular bill and its intent confirms it for the present and entrenches it for the future. It could not be said better.
On the other hand, I think the opposition members in this House, together with the native people, particularly those in the north and on the west coast, are determined to break that colonial status. They want to share adequately by defining their interest in that area and by having the government acknowledge it and provide action in good faith. The land is of interest and so are the forest and mining resources. But we must not forget the sea. The native people of western Canada have a long tradition with the sea in the area immediately adjacent to the west coast. Defining that will be a complex problem. The resources in the sea are seriously affected by all this activity. We need a provision in this legislation which stops the alienation process before the land claim is developed.
I would urge members to travel through the native communities located on the west coast. The inhabitants like to talk about the place where they live. They like to talk about themselves and their history. Native people are very close to their parents and their grandparents. Tradition is handed down through generations. For instance, the way the land and the sea is used is locked into an oral history that has been transmitted down through families in great detail and with great consistency. You can travel down a fjord in a boat with the west coast natives of British Columbia, you can pass a point and they will tell you that their ancestors used to live there. They will tell you what they did, but it always relates to the sea. Marine resources are the base of that civilization. The history and mythology of the natives which have been transmitted through the generations really develops a land claim. People, both old and young alike, who live and work out there can tell you all about these people and what they did. History is the base upon which these claims will develop, but it will take a lot of time. There is a great deal of archeological evidence which confirms the oral history, the interest in the land and the marine environment.
Some bands have a very high level of development. They have established land claims and they are working diligently toward defining them. But this is very difficult to do. Some bands do not have even basic means of day-to-day survival. All of their resources are committed to that survival and they are certainly inadequate. They do not have resources to begin to
October 19, 1981

work out a land claim or to begin to negotiate with the government. But two years from now holes will be punched in the sea bed. There is even talk about exploring river beds. Obviously they are hoping to find oil and gas. What the government legislation proposes is to allow that development to proceed quickly. This would have an impact environmentally, socially and economically without giving adequate protection to the native people who need time to define their claims, to develop their resources and so begin to negotiate with the government. That is a big mistake. We have heard from the native people, from opposition members, from church groups. In fact, a whole range of people in the Canadian society have brought the concerns of the native people forward. But the government has said, "Enough, discretion is all right". The government says to us, "Trust us, it is in the mail." But that is simply not good enough. This is a very complex area in respect of which the assurance of the government is needed. We need an assurance that the government will recognize the principle put forward in the previous member's motion. If the government had come forward and opened up in a forthright manner, a lot of the delay this bill has seen could have been avoided. That delay could have been avoided by a statement of principle and a clear expression of the government's intent.
Let me give you an example. We who worked in that media unfortunately had to resort to a filibuster and to delaying tactics. This was extremely hard on everyone, including government members who had to sit there and listen. But our goals were very specific. The investor benefit section was vital. We needed some definition. The government had a program all along. We asked them to hold a closed meeting if they were afraid the information would get out, but to let us know in that way how the government intended to provide protection. We wanted the government to show us some developments or mechanisms such as the British offshore supply office. We wanted the government to put this into the legislation and to do something specific rather than just to ask us to trust it. First, we cannot trust the government, and history would indicate it is often going in another direction.
After weeks of battling, by gosh, the government said, "Okay, you win. We will have an in camera session". It was good. However, the government just would not express the principles to be used or demonstrate the mechanisms so that one could have some confidence that Canadian interest would be protected.
We face the same thing here with this motion. The drafting of the amendment may not be the best. There are certain aspects that I would question, but on the other side of the coin there is the vital principle that the government must do more because this whole question of trust is lost. There is nothing in this on which the native people can hang their hats. We want a definition because too much has been lost in 200 years.
I would guess, casting my mind back a bit in history, that the west coast in British Columbia was run by three Indian chiefs; Tatoosh who lived at Cape Flattery, Wichininesh who

lived in the old Nanaimo-Alberni riding at Long Beach, now the federal park, Pacific Rim, and another chief, Maquinug, who lived at Friendly Cove. They ran the west coast of Vancouver Island. The descendants of the Hilson people were here today trying to talk to ministers of the Crown. Reputedly, their ancestors travelled from Hawaii and Polynesia. They lived in a community called Waglisla. The sea is the resource that supported all those people. There is a tremendous history of the native people in western Canada. There is a long relationship with the land and sea, and there is a belief that if we give the native people an opportunity, they can define, substantiate, share and participate, as the rest of us hope to share and participate, in the benefits of those resources.
The colonial system that was imposed on them from the time of Cooke and Alexander Mackenzie and the others who came was very clear. These native people lost their access to the forests to the major forestry companies; MacMillan Bloe-del, Dorman, Rayonier and IT & T. All of them now own the forests of British Columbia and the Indian people have been dispossessed. The Indian people used to have a large number of fishing vessels, but Jack Davis and subsequent ministers have taken away those vessels, and now most of them are on the beach. The wealthy white men from other walks of life, the moonlighters and interlopers, have now taken the fishing industry away from them, and the native people are now on the beach. They have lost their resource base; they have lost access to the sea. The Indian people have lost access to the forest. The provincial government has cut them off from their traditional resource base. Their actual reserve lands on which they live have been cut down.
