speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to support strongly the motion of the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Schellenberger), and I hope to prove to hon. members on the government side why they too should support this motion, particularly if they are sincere with regard to that which is already in the bill.
Let me refer to the motion which would add, "nothing in this act abrogates", and that means repeals or cancels, or "derogates", which means detracts or takes away, from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this act. When I read the second paragraph I see that it says the governor in council may by order-not in this House but by order-for any purpose or any condition set out in the order, withdraw from the application of this act such Canada lands as are specified in the order. It is all-embracive. The amendment simply states that any claim or interests the aboriginal people have will not be withdrawn; that is, the lands will not be withdrawn. How can the government refuse to support that amendment if it believes in that which already exists in the bill? If Section 2 is to become all-embracive and have power over the other sections because it comes before, then there is a very serious and severe contradiction in the legislation.
That is not the only thing which disturbs me about this bill. I do not really know what the policy of the government is with regard to our aboriginal people. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that prior to January, 1981, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked to include aboriginal rights in the Charter of Rights by a member on this side of the House. The Prime Minister said that he would in no way include aboriginal rights in the charter unless he knew what aboriginal rights meant, unless aboriginal rights were defined. That is the gist of what the Prime Minister said. In January, 1981, a provision on the rights of the aboriginal people was placed in Section 34(1). It reads;
The aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
I reiterate, "recognized and affirmed". Now I would like to know if the Prime Minister has a definition of aboriginal
rights. I think it is important that he have such a definition because when I started looking into government policy I was astounded to find an order in council which set out government policy in regard to aboriginal claims, that is an order in council dated August 8, 1973, which has not yet been either discharged or denounced by the Liberal government. It is still in force. If it is in force, then Subclause (7) of this bill is meaningless. I will read what the order in council says:
__the government will negotiate claims and settle claims according to the policy
in the Annual Report of the Department of Indian Affairs.
It simply says the government will negotiate a settlement with the Indian and Inuit people who have not entered into treaty relationships with the Crown. These settlements will be based upon the loss of their traditional use and occupancy of lands in those parts of Canada where native rights, based on traditional use and occupancy, have not been extinguished by treaty or superseded by law.
In other words, the government has set out three caveats in that order in council, which is still on the books, with respect to the claims of Indian and Inuit people. The first one is that the government will only negotiate and settle claims based on land and occupancy of land. In other words, the whole culture of the Indian and Inuit people will be ignored unless they live on the land, unless they have already placed a claim on that particular land and occupy it. There is no consideration for negotiation whatsoever. That is set out in law. Consequently, the amendment to this bill will mean nothing. The government will simply point to the order in council of August 8, 1973, which still stands.
What do we mean by aboriginal rights? Aboriginal rights go beyond land occupied. Most Inuit and Indian people, or at least many of them, make their living by hunting and fishing. They do not live on those lands, they hunt and fish on them. They do not occupy them by building a house on them, in that sense of occupation. The rights they had when the white man first came to this land, such as their language, their dances and their political social and economic cultures, all of these are part and parcel of aboriginal rights. They are being ignored in this section. It deals only with land, and even then there is a caveat placed on the land-that they must occupy it. They must have already had a claim to it. I think the Inuit and Indian people should take careful note and find out about this policy mentioned in the charter of rights and find out if it has not already been lost before the charter of rights is passed.
The next caveat set out in the order in council says that the government will only negotiate and settle claims which have not been extinguished by treaty. When the government, for example, negotiates with the Inuit or Indian people for a number of years, it insists that the Indian and Inuit people give up all rights; those held in the past, those they have currently, those they might have in the future, all rights not specifically extinguished by agreement. Well, that is going too far. I suggest that is a caveat the Indian and Inuit people would want discarded before the section in the charter means very much.
October 19, 1981

There is a third caveat: the government will only negotiate and settle claims which have not been superseded by law. If any government, provincial or federal, since the beginning of this country, has passed any act or bill or order in council taking away a right from the Inuit or Indian people, then the government will not negotiate. They will not even talk about it. Again, I suggest to our Indian and Inuit Canadians that they take a very careful look at all the enactments since the beginning of confederation to find out whether they will have any right to make a claim or even if they can negotiate. What does that piece in the charter say? It says:
The aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
What does the order in council say? It says that the government will not negotiate unless the Indian and Inuit people make a claim and occupy the land. They will not negotiate unless the traditional use and occupancy have not been extinguished by treaty. They will not negotiate if any part of that has been superseded by any law or enactment or order in council.
Where does that leave our Indian and Inuit Canadians? Does this section in our Charter of Rights pull the wool over the eyes of our Indian and Inuit people, in the hope of pushing it through before they find out all these things? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if this government is sincere in giving aboriginal rights to our Indian and Inuit people, our native peoples, they would define aboriginal rights and denounce and discharge the order in council which was passed on August 8, 1973. If their policy means anything, let the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) or the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stand up and say that the order in council has been annulled and discharged. They should stand up and say that they will annul and discharge that order in council and they should even pass another order in council that it is no longer the policy of the government. Then the Indian and Inuit people might have some hope of getting a fair and equal settlement. Ever since white men came to this country, the Indian and Inuit people have been exploited. We have not given them an opportunity to develop their skills. Even now our education system does not go far enough. The withdrawal of Outreach funds by the government will have a detrimental effect on the Outreach programs on at least one reserve of which I know in my constituency and I do not know on how many others across the country. The Outreach program of the University of Calgary on the Stoney reserve has done a tremendous job, with the result that young people there have been able to get the necessary basic training to go to university. Some have graduated with degrees and today are playing their part in developing this country. However, cutting back funds will affect that Outreach program. We have exploited them; let us not continue to try to pull the wool over their eyes.
I ask this government to denounce this order in council program it has been following and to be above board. Let us put the record straight, let us say we will leave all that in the
Canada Oil and Gas Act
past and we will now define aboriginal rights with the help of the Indian and Inuit people, in a way which is fair to everyone.
That is all our Indian and Inuit people are asking for. If the government will not do that, I for one will be very apprehensive about anything it says about aboriginal rights.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too should like to address myself to the rights of the native peoples of Canada. Only a little while ago the constitutional resolution proclaimed the aboriginal rights of the native peoples of this country which the present Bill C-48 denies. I therefore support not only the amendment before us but, indeed, other amendments my party has brought forward.
I am delighted to see the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Joyal), now a minister of state, here in the House tonight because it was he, as co-chairman of the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on the constitutional resolution-

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Who was the other co-chairman?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: I have forgotten.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: How soon we forget.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
It was he, as I understand it-I may be misled-who gave encouragement to the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) and other members of this party to press for the introduction into the constitutional resolution of Section 34(1), already referred to this evening, in which the aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
When the government acceded to the amendment this party proposed, one part of which included the strengthening of the aboriginal and treaty rights of the native peoples of Canada, it was my understanding that at least this co-chairman, and perhaps both co-chairmen, of the constitutional committee were enthusiastic and anxious to see this clause entrenched. That is not to say that the clause is perfect, but most of us thought then, and still think, that the courts are likely to give this clause paramountcy; that the fears of many of the native peoples of Canada that their rights will still be denied them are, we hope, not genuine fears; that they are not real; that they need not fear; and that we feel that the clause will be respected and given paramountcy by the courts.
But what happens to an hon. member when he joins the cabinet? I congratulate the minister on his appointment, but what happens? Either he has not studied the bill before us and the amendments before us or, if he has studied them, he has not realized that the bill itself absolutely denies the very aboriginal rights that he and all of us, at least in this party, spent so much time affirming. It seems to me that this is giving with one hand only to take away with the other. The very same thing could have happened, and the minister responsible for the status of women today assured us it would not happen, as far as native women are concerned. If I heard correctly today in the House, she said we would not wait for the three-year moratorium period, assuming the constitutional resolution is

October 19, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
passed, before we ensure that the inequities now in Section 12(l)(b) of the Indian Act are removed. Yet at the very moment one minister of the Crown is saying we will not continue with these inequities, the government, in a related field, namely, all matters relating to land claims, fishing and hunting rights and so forth, is saying we will perpetuate injustice, unfairness and inequities.
I urge the Minister of State, the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, before it is too late to bring his voice to bear in cabinet and elsewhere to ensure that the amendments which have been proposed and are still to be proposed will in fact be looked at much more seriously by the government. It will be too late, as far as the native people of Canada are concerned, when exploration and development has surged into the area of the Canada lands with no serious regard for the needs of the native peoples of this country or for their wishes or their genuine concerns, which we all say we share. If the government does not act now, it will be much too late, so I urge the minister, just as his colleague today said she would urge the government, to take steps immediately to rectify the inequities caused by Section 12(l)(b). I urge him to take the same steps with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and, indeed, with the whole government.
Similarly, I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan), who was here a moment ago, will also involve himself in this question of native rights. Hon. members might think this is not a matter which would ordinarily concern the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I agree that he has a great many other concerns, but I know that the last thing he would want or, indeed, any of us want, would be another reference to the United Nations Human Rights Commission comparable to the Sandra Lovelace case. This case, however, concerns deprivation of the rights of the native peoples of Canada and particularly the right to have land claims and other claims negotiated. I cannot say for sure that could come before the United Nations commission, but it might come before it.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER RECONSIDER DECISION ON FUTURE OF PASSENGER SERVICES
REQUEST THAT MINISTER RECONSIDER DECISION ON FUTURE OF PASSENGER SERVICES
speechtext:
On October 14 I posed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), arising out of his announced statement of July 27 cutting back VIA Rail services by 19 per cent, and affecting some 1.2 million passengers and, particularly, some 1,600 railway workers, plus countless other jobs which will be indirectly affected as a result of the cutbacks.
I asked the minister to reconsider seriously this illogical and shortsighted arbitrary decision, given the fact that we are in serious difficulty with the economy. Unemployment is running at a high rate. The cutbacks will affect the areas of Canada that experience the highest level of unemployment.
The reply the minister gave confirms to my colleagues and myself that little thought had gone into the social and economic impact of such a decision on the workers and their families, particularly in the eastern and western regions of Canada. They will feel a tremendous impact from the cutback of the transportation services which are needed and used.
The minister said he would be prepared to come before the committee to explain his decision; but he did not say he would be prepared to defer the decision. That is simply not good enough, Mr. Speaker.
He also suggested we could have dealt with this matter under our broad terms of reference that was issued by the House with regard to the study of transportation matters in Quebec and Ontario, which the Standing Committee on Transportation undertook this summer. The minister knows very well the mandate was limited. It dealt only with transportation matters in the province of Quebec and Ontario. The cutbacks we are dealing with affect all of Canada, not only the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. We had limited time. This being a national issue, it requires a lot more study and a lot more time than the minister is prepared to give it.
In the response of the minister we are simply being given a whitewash. He will come before the committee, wax eloquent and try to explain his position, without hearing the other side of the story. This is simply not good enough. Lay-off notices, Mr. Speaker, have already been issued. CN in Montreal
October 19, 1981

announced for the first of September that some 560 positions will be affected by the cutbacks of VIA Rail; two fifths of the positions in Montreal, two fifths in Winnipeg, and the balance in Moncton. VIA Rail has issued lay-off notices; 133 in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, 166 in western Canada, some in Ontario and a few others in administrative and accounting positions. This works out to 313 people.
The cutbacks, Mr. Speaker, occur in areas of high unemployment; mainly the province of Quebec, the Atlantic region and in western Canada, particularly in the city of Winnipeg where the bulk of the lay-offs will take place. There are other matters, Mr. Speaker. I am sure the minister, his officials and his cabinet colleagues did not consider the tremendous impact this will have on the future economic development opportunities both in the west and in the maritimes with regard to tourism.
Japanese tourists rely very heavily upon the use of rail service. They are big spenders. They are major contributors to Canada's balance of payments, particularly with the large amount of money they spend. The Canadian government tourist office suggests that the Japanese spend an average of $2,000 per capita when they come to visit the country. This is in addition to the payment for their travel and their hotels. Altogether, some 25,000 Japanese visitors travel through western Canada by train. We are looking at a potential loss of some $50 million if those opportunities are gone.
The minister also suggested that he will save some $100 million. We challenge that figure just as we challenge the statement that he could revitalize rail passenger services by abandonment. In short, he will not achieve that saving. The $30 million will be paid out immediately for adjustments, relocations and training programs for the people who will be laid off.
The actions of the minister constitute a very dangerous precedent. If he is absolutely sure his decision is correct, I challenge him to take his decision to the public and let the court of the Canadian public judge it. If he did, he may be apprised of the tremendous hardships and sufferings his decision will inflict upon hundreds of thousands of Canadians across the country.
The minister's act constitutes a very dangerous precedent, in my view. I hate to say this, but by virtue of the fact that the minister refuses to go through the normal and traditional process of public hearings, either through the Canadian Transport Commission or through a parliamentary committee, what he is doing constitutes a cowardly act. I hope he will reconsider the action he has taken and will allow the committee to study this matter. In order for it to be studied properly and fully, he must defer the decision. I plead and urge the minister to do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER RECONSIDER DECISION ON FUTURE OF PASSENGER SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the cabinet made a decision to implement a reduction of rail passenger services in Canada which would
Adjournment Debate
create operating economies in order that these savings might be used for the purpose of acquiring new passenger trains and equipment for both the Atlantic and the western provinces. By reducing the operating deficits of VIA, the capital budget would correspondingly experience an increase.
I have with me notes for an address by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) to the Canadian Transportation Research Forum on June 11,1980, in which he said:
On the passenger side of rail transportation, the ever-increasing debt incurred by the federal government in subsidies is a major problem which will have to be dealt with. This fiscal year alone, $424 million will go toward subsidizing rail passenger service. This is especially urgent when considering the impact on rail's competition, the bus mode.
The hon. member for Vegreville understated the problem because in 1980, seven million VIA Rail passenger tickets were sold and the subsidies amounted to $490 million.
We have in Canada two transcontinental services. The intention is to reduce them to one line to avoid a duplication of services. The transcontinental services account for more than half the operating deficit. The second transcontinental service will be replaced by daytime intercity services. Alternatives are therefore being put forward by the government. The cabinet has considered this matter three or four times. It was a difficult decision to reach, and the cabinet has no intention of reversing it.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the president of the Toronto-Havelock Line Passenger Association said in his organization's submission to the Progressive Conservative task force on VIA Rail and the all-party committee on transport:
It is absurd to believe that VIA Rail will actually revitalize Canada's rail-passenger service by discontinuing service, especially the most promising one. By careful study, subsidies to the retained routes are found to be as much as 13 times greater than the stated subsidy to the Toronto-Peterborough-Havelock service.
It can be proved beyond a reasonable doubt that VIA Rail's revenues have been understated. It is further suspected that deficits have been purposely inflated by a disproportionate allocation of costs to passenger trains-costs that should rightly be charged to freight operations.
With that in mind-and I would add, incidentally, that the association's opinion has been endorsed by an actuary who reviewed the route's fiscal situation-it was particularly distressing to me last Thursday, October 15, when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) refused my request in the House that the figures he uses to justify the termination of VIA Rail service-19 per cent of the service in Canada-be audited.
As he had tentatively agreed, at least, to appear in person before the Standing Committee on Transport to justify cutting Canada's rail-passenger network by 19 per cent, I was hopeful that he would, in addition, agree to allowing the costing procedures he used to justify the Toronto-Havelock route to be audited. Very serious questions have been raised with regard to these figures and out of a total yearly sum of approximately

October 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
$350,000 which is involved on that line, some $100,000 or thereabouts is in question.
On Thursday, the minister sidestepped the specific question with regard to the cost justification on the Toronto-Havelock route by claiming that he viewed the route, and others in Ontario, as essentially of a "commuter" nature. This is despite a clear understanding which the minister shared with Mr. Snow, the minister of transportation and communications for Ontario. Mr. Snow was good enough to forward to me a letter of his where he said that the Minister of Transport concurred that the Toronto-Havelock service is intercity in nature and is being dropped because of the losses it is incurring".
Now we have two elements in the dispute over this particular route. First, is it essentially a commuter-route or an intercity service? Second, are the losses which the route is allegedly incurring enough to shut it down? The minister has since said that this route is "-dominated by commuter traffic and cannot be justified as intercity service if the commuter element is removed". That is to say, the route as it stands now is an inter-city type service because quite clearly the "commuter-element" can hardly be practically removed and constitutes merely a semantic sleight-of-hand which the minister's officials are so obviously reduced to. How on earth can the "commuter-element" possibly be removed? This is quite absurd. There is obviously a "commuter-element" on virtually every passenger train in the country.
The minister also refers in his letter to the published CTC decision contained in Order R-32317, where it found that the Rail Transport Committee "-intends to review this case with the purpose of deciding whether or not the Toronto-Havelock Service should continue to be designated as a passenger-train service".
I do not see why this justifies the minister's precipitous action. It is the function and purpose of the CTC Rail Transport Committee and not that of Transport Canada or the minister's office to decide whether or not it is indeed a passenger-train service. If the minister wants to discuss the CTC order, let him discuss the order's final recommendation which reads as follows:
Accordingly, it is the decision of the committee that... the Toronto-Havelock service shall not be discontinued.
They reached this decision despite having weighed the same evidence as has the minister, presumably.
However, the minister finally admits in his letter to me that:
It is the type of traffic rather than the losses they are incurring which led the government to terminate (the line).
In that case, I suppose we need not squabble about that odd $100,000 which the minister so airily dismisses, and concentrate on the route's "traffic". The minister's definition here deserves close scrutiny, preferably by the rail transport committee of the CTC, or at least by Parliament's Standing Committee on Transport, for as the rail passenger association's brief describes:
1)	Less than 50 per cent of passengers and less than 20 per cent of revenues can be attributed to commuters travelling within the Metropolitan Toronto region.
2)	The average number of passengers carried per train on this particular service equals or exceeds the average number per train on the Quebec City-Windsor corridor services.
This House needs a full explanation from the Minister of Transport as to why he refuses to have his figures audited or questioned by the CTC, and why he has resorted to an order in council to terminate 19 per cent of our passenger rail service in Canada without a public hearing and against the wishes of the CTC and an all-party standing committee on transportation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in its decision of May 29, 1981, the CTC had strong reason to believe that the Toronto-Havelock service might be essentially commuter in nature and therefore not entitled to subsidies because the Railway Act does not provide for the subsidization of commuter services.
Havelock is 101 miles from Toronto. Havelock service is, however, commuter traffic dominated. VIA Rail conducted a survey of the Toronto-Havelock service earlier this year. On a typical work day, ten people boarded the train in Havelock and 239 disembarked at the Union Station in Toronto from the westbound train; the reverse was true on the eastbound train. VIA found that 55 per cent of the passengers board at the last two stops closest to Toronto; namely, Agincourt and Leaside. Only 25 per cent of the passengers using this train service go beyond Burketon, which is 47 miles from Toronto.
It is the type of traffic which led the government to its decision to terminate subsidy payments on the line in question. It was recognized that these trains perform an important function for commuters. The date of termination was set one year in advance to give the government of Ontario ample notice that it might integrate these services into its own commuter network.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FISHERIES-STATE OF INDUSTRY IN SOUTHERN NOVA SCOTIA
FISHERIES-STATE OF INDUSTRY IN SOUTHERN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was asked on June 2, 1981, of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). I do not want to repeat the question, but it related to the state of the industry in the southern end of Nova Scotia. I am sure that many people consider this to be one of the best fishing areas in eastern Canada.
The history, goes back prior to my question. It was on April 6, 1981, that I first asked the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans if he would set up an independent study group of fishermen and processors, big and small, as well as one economist, to study the distressing situation in the process of one month that was developing. Of course, no study was done, and I think what happened in June and July was a result of that.
The fishermen did come and meet with the Fisheries Prices Support Board, and I must say that we were well received; so well received that one has to look at what we got out of it. We got a $14 million fisheries prices stabilization program for
October 19, 1981

haddock, announced on July 24, 1981, approximately four months from the time I first spoke in the House concerning the crisis. This price support was on future inventory, not on past inventory. Therefore, the cost to the processors of storing the inventory under this program was of no consequence at all because it was kept back so that prices would increase in the marketplace.
This was not well received by either the fishermen or the industry. Nor has it been acted upon. In addition, 1981 was a very poor year. It all started back between January and May, 1981, with the haddock catches. At that time of the year only the offshore fleets on the east coast are fishing and many plants are in operation. I am sure the hon. parliamentary secretary knows of plants operating last year during a period when they normally do not operate.
In the maritimes from January to May, 1980, the catch increased from 14,000 pounds to upwards of 19,500 pounds. In Newfoundland, the catch increased from 1,500 pounds to 5,200 pounds. No wonder the plants were working when they normally would not have been, no wonder there was no fish on the east coast later in the year, and no wonder that in southern Nova Scotia, even if there was fish, there was no market for it because there was a glut in haddock. Prices to fishermen went down at that time from 25 cents, which was the lowest last year, to 17 cents in May and June of this year. Prices have not gone up that much even though no haddock was being caught in that area except for the months of August and September.
We can blame marketing conditions on the province, on industry and on the federal government. I would say that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans should be hitting very hard on the marketing end at the federal level. But then he turned to quality. I have something to say about that. It is not, in my view, a global statement as indicated in his press release from Marystown, which reads that all fish should be bled and gutted and that the minister wished that the five provincial ministers of fishery would implement this regulation.
At the beginning of September the federal government funded a $14 million stabilization program, virtually saying that the offshore fleet does not have any fish to supply to the plants. "Therefore," they said, "We will let them open up early and we will give them additional quotas because the scientists have found that this year there are more fish for the big offshore fleet to catch." If they have so much additional pollock or cod quotas they will also have a by-catch of haddock of 10 per cent. But when will that take place? It will take place in September and October, which is the last period of the year when our fishermen have the best of the season to fish. But prices are depressed, both the price of haddock to the fishermen and prices to the small processors. Because the catches are not high, the plant workers will have insufficient unemployment insurance stamps as a result of this terrible glut which started at the beginning of the year and ended with the department bringing in a $14 million stabilization program. Then another branch of the department, under the fisheries
Adjournment Debate
management plan, amended the plan halfway through the year allowing the offshore fleets to return to the inshore waters to capture additional quotas which they felt was their due and just reward. They could not wait until October 15. They had to go then.
This is a prime example of government departments not finding out what one is doing on the one hand and what the other is doing on the other hand.
I would like to state now that quality will not enhance marketing conditions as far as fishermen in the southern end of the province are concerned unless the department, instead of just issuing quality improvement directives, indicates what we need and what will bring the prices up. You cannot go to a group of fishermen who are icing and whose fish has commanded the best of price right across the land and say they have to do something different when they are out for two days at the most with good icing facilities on their boats and when the local plants are receiving the highest prices, and when the only reason quality is perhaps not so good is that the big multinationals do not have the same quality standards as some of the smaller businesses.
The fact that I have to stand here tonight compounds the fact that the issue has been before this House since last April. I feel very strongly that the department should have a handle on this issue. It does not have a handle on the situation over the entire season. We are now coming up to the time of new quotas with a new season starting in January with depressed markets, and the department has done nothing, in my view, to cure the situation by its policies over the summer, particularly those of price stabilization from the Fisheries Prices Support Board. This could have been good except that the inventory being bought was future inventory and there was not that much to buy at the time. The department then allowed the offshore fleet to come in in September, depressing prices that should have been going up at that time. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-STATE OF INDUSTRY IN SOUTHERN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to tell the member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) that I appreciate her concern and very earnest representation on behalf of her constituents. Indeed, it has been a difficult year everywhere in fisheries in eastern Canada, and I know that in Newfoundland in many cases the bottom fell out of the cod market.
The hon. member mentioned quality several times during her comments. I became aware of an interesting fact some time ago which I think illustrates the need for quality in the fisheries in Atlantic Canada and, indeed, on the west coast of Canada as well. The total world production of fish and seafood is 74 million tonnes. Canada produces just one million tonnes. We are not in a position to assume we have some kind of monopoly in respect of fish and seafood. Indeed, we do have to prepare a quality product if we want to get to world markets.

October 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
The state of the fishing industry in southern Nova Scotia has been characterized by a glut of haddock products on the U.S. market which is causing low prices to both Canadian and U.S. fishermen. Canadian haddock landings have risen from
19,000	tonnes in 1976 to 51,000 tonnes in 1980, with landed value ranging from $8 million to $25 million during the same period. U.S. landings have increased almost four times from 1976 to 1980. During the January-July period, 1981, Canadian haddock landings were 30 per cent higher than in the similar period of last year. Prices for haddock to the southwest Nova Scotia fishermen were as high as 35 cents per pound, round, earlier this year, but have dropped to approximately 17 cents in May and June and increased to 19 cents per pound last September.
An additional factor in the oversupplied U.S. market is increased haddock block shipments from Norway and Iceland,
haddock that is marketed in competition with our products. Here is where quality once again comes into question. Southern Nova Scotia fishermen as well are affected by the recent decline of cod prices received. The U.S. cod market has been dull in recent months and has affected all of eastern Canada.
I should like to say in closing that, at the request of the industry, the Fisheries Prices Support Board reviewed the situation in June and was authorized, effective July 25, 1981, to implement a price stabilization program for haddock. The board continues to monitor the situation with respect to haddock and, I assure you, with respect to other species as well.
